### THE GAME OF MARBLES

<!-- rl-section id="section-31" class="epub-section" kicker="Section 31" title="17" -->

## 17

## The Mother and Father of All Evil

> *The dollar is our currency but your problem.*
>
> US Treasury Secretary John Connally, 1971

### THE DOLLAR STANDARD

Interest rates have always regulated international capital flows. In the era of the Gold Standard, this job was done automatically. If the Bank of England brought rates much below foreign levels, gold would leave its vaults for foreign shores. ‘Loanable capital, like every other commodity, comes where there is most to be made of it,’ wrote Bagehot of Victorian lending practices. In order to attract gold back to the City of London, the Bank of England would have had to raise its lending rate. After the Bretton Woods system collapsed in 1971, the US dollar became the global reserve currency. After this date most international trade was denominated in the US currency, along with a large share of cross-border financial transactions. Dozens of countries pegged their own currencies to the dollar.

If the Gold Standard was characterized by its ‘golden fetters’, the chief vice of the Dollar Standard is its extreme elasticity. Central bank reserves are mostly composed of dollar-denominated securities (US Treasury bonds and agency debt), which, unlike gold, can be issued without limit. As the keeper of the world’s reserve currency, the United States doesn’t need to maintain its own foreign-exchange reserves, nor worry about its balance of payments. There is no limit on how many dollars flow abroad nor how much the United States borrows from foreigners. America can run what Jacques Rueff called ‘deficits without tears’, and over the years it has taken advantage of this exorbitant privilege to become the world’s largest international debtor.

US interest rates aren’t influenced by international capital flows. Absent the prospect of inflation, there is no limit on how low interest rates can sink. (The question of whether the Fed could set negative rates is murky from a legal perspective.) Not everything has changed, however. Differentials in interest rates between countries still influence the amount and direction of cross-border lending. The most important interest-rate spread is that between the cost of borrowing in the United States and elsewhere. Countries that peg their currencies to the dollar are obliged to shadow American monetary policy: they must loosen when the Fed loosens and tighten when the Fed tightens. When the US central bank eases, dollar-peggers often intervene in the foreign exchanges: to prevent their currencies from appreciating, their central banks buy dollars with freshly printed local currency, thereby further loosening domestic monetary conditions.

In short, when the United States adopts easy money it unleashes a ‘global monetary plague’.[1](#section-53) The plague is not contained to countries which peg to the dollar: even those with floating currencies are infected. When US interest rates fall below foreign rates, international carry trades take off. Investors borrow dollars and invest the proceeds abroad at higher yields. Foreigners are also encouraged to take out cheap dollar-denominated loans. (The yen and euro are also commonly used to finance cross-border carry trades.) For instance, when Iceland’s economy overheated in the early 2000s its central bank raised rates. But high Icelandic rates attracted hordes of carry traders who borrowed in foreign currencies (dollars, euros and yen) to acquire krona-denominated securities, known as ‘glacier bonds’, and lent directly to Icelandic banks, thereby easing, rather than tightening, monetary conditions.[2](#section-53)

### THE FIRST PHASE OF GLOBAL LIQUIDITY

The early years of this century witnessed a remarkable growth in central bank reserves. Conventional wisdom maintains that the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves indicated a ‘global savings glut’. Emerging markets were said to be amassing reserves in order to protect themselves against another Asian-style crisis. But the link between the growth of foreign exchange reserves and ‘excess savings’ (i.e., current account surpluses) is tenuous.[3](#section-53) Several countries, including Turkey, expanded their foreign reserves while running current account deficits. Some economists, including John Taylor of Stanford, found no evidence that the global savings rate had actually increased.

An alternative account holds that the world in the early years of the new millennium was suffering a surfeit of finance – a ‘global banking glut’.[4](#section-53) According to this interpretation, the Greenspan Fed’s easy money stimulated a rise in cross-border capital flows, which increased threefold in the first years of the century.[5](#section-53) This explosion of international lending fuelled a global credit bubble.[6](#section-53) Countries which operated a dollar peg responded to the surge in capital inflows by acquiring the incoming dollars. Hence, the extraordinary increase in foreign exchange reserves.

As the world’s reserve currency, the US dollar served as the main funding currency for international carry trades. European banks borrowed in the New York money markets to acquire subprime securities. Europe had its own carry trades. Cross-border bank loans financed Greece’s enormous current account deficit and real estate booms in Spain and Ireland.[7](#section-53) Foreign lending to Central Europe topped $1 trillion in 2007, enabling Romanian credit to grow at an annualized rate of 66 per cent, financing a Latvian current account deficit to the tune of a quarter of GDP, and allowing Poles and Hungarians to take out cheap mortgages, denominated in euros and Swiss francs.[8](#section-53) By the onset of the global financial crisis, Iceland’s foreign debts had grown to nearly nine times its national output.[fn1](#section-58)

### THE SECOND PHASE OF GLOBAL LIQUIDITY

The financial convulsions of 2007–8 may have been triggered by losses on American subprime mortgages, but it’s more accurate to describe the global crisis as a ‘giant carry trade gone wrong’.[fn2](#section-58) After Lehman’s bankruptcy, foreign banks which had borrowed dollars to buy US mortgage securities lost access to the international money markets. The Federal Reserve came to their rescue, providing massive lines of dollar credit to central banks in Europe and Asia. Chairman Bernanke’s prompt actions prevented a collapse of the global monetary system, as had occurred in the early 1930s.[9](#section-53)

But this very success, combined with the move to zero interest rates at the core of the global financial system, revived the international carry trade. Economist Hyun Song Shin of the BIS coined the term the ‘second phase of global liquidity’ to describe the resurgence of international capital flows after 2008. Both phases of global liquidity were characterized by abnormally low interest rates in the United States, low levels of market volatility (as measured by the VIX) and extensive cross-border lending.[10](#section-53) In the first phase, international capital flows financed credit booms and real estate bubbles on the edges of Europe. In the second phase, foreign capital mostly poured into emerging markets. In the first phase, the financial systems on the periphery of Europe became dangerously exposed. In the second phase, financial weakness spread throughout the developing world.

The second phase of global liquidity got off to an explosive start. Over the course of 2009, emerging market bond funds witnessed record inflows.[11](#section-53) The IMF observed in November that the dollar was ‘now serving as the funding currency for carry trades’.[12](#section-53) New York University economist Nouriel Roubini issued a starker warning. The combination of easy money, quantitative easing and a weakening dollar had produced the ‘mother of all carry trades’, said Roubini:

> But one day this bubble will burst, leading to the biggest coordinated asset bust ever … the longer and bigger the carry trades and the larger the asset bubble, the bigger will be the ensuing asset bubble crash. The Fed and other policymakers seem unaware of the monster bubble they are creating. The longer they remain blind, the harder the markets will fall.[13](#section-53)

Of more immediate concern to policymakers in emerging markets was the rapid appreciation of their currencies, induced by a weak dollar and unconstrained capital inflows. Brazil’s Finance Minister Guido Mantega complained that the United States was engaged in a currency war. To discourage hot money flows, Mantega announced a tax on foreign purchases of Brazilian stocks and bonds. Central banks in the developing world played a defensive role in the currency wars, intervening in the currency markets to buy dollars. In the process they added greatly to their foreign exchange reserves. By 2013 global foreign exchange reserves were touching $12 trillion, up from $2 trillion at the turn of the century. (Since trade imbalances were shrinking, there was now less talk of any global savings glut.)

Massive purchases of dollar securities by central banks put downward pressure on US Treasury yields. Foreign exchange interventions by central banks, combined with hot money flows and increased lending by state banks (notably in China, India and Brazil), eased credit conditions across the emerging markets; as did the fact that their domestic interest rates were falling, drawn downwards by the gravitational pull of zero interest rates at the heart of the world’s financial system.[14](#section-53) Inflation started to pick up across the emerging markets. By early 2010, the BRICs – Goldman Sachs’ catchy acronym for Brazil, Russia, India and China – were overheating.[15](#section-53) In October, rubber and cotton futures jumped to record levels. Arabica coffee prices hit a thirteen-year high. Flooding across South East Asia affected the rice harvest, driving up rice futures by more than 50 per cent.[16](#section-53)

### THE ARAB SPRING

On 17 December 2010, a young Tunisian street vendor doused his clothes with petrol and set himself alight outside the Governor’s office in the provincial town of Sidi Bouzid. Mohamed Bouazizi committed suicide in protest against the actions of local police who had confiscated his wares and smashed his cart. The day after his death riots broke out in Sidi Bouzid. Unrest spread rapidly across North Africa and the Middle East. Within a month Tunisian President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali had been forced from office, followed soon after by the departure of Libya’s Colonel Gaddafi and Egypt’s Hosni Mubarak.

Like many popular uprisings in history, the Arab Spring started out as a bread riot.[17](#section-53) Over the course of the year, world cereal prices climbed by 29 per cent.[18](#section-53) Bouazizi earned his pittance selling vegetables, which might explain why corrupt officials were keen to appropriate his wares. North Africa, once the grain basket of the Roman Empire, was now the world’s largest food importer. Half of Egypt’s wheat – the main staple for the country’s 80 million-odd population – came from abroad. A much-photographed protester in Cairo’s Tahrir Square wore a ‘bread helmet’ made from a croissant and two bread sticks held together with cling film. Commentators blamed crop failures among the world’s leading food exporters on climate change.

But some other factor must have contributed to the sharp rise in food prices, since the price of industrial commodities, whose supply was unaffected by the weather, also soared in the months prior to the Arab Spring. Most industrial commodities, and precious metals from copper to silver, were trading at bubble levels.[fn3](#section-58) That additional factor was the Federal Reserve’s monetary policies. Stanford economist Ronald McKinnon argued that the Arab Spring originated with ultra-low interest rates in the United States, which, as we have seen, drove capital flows into the emerging world and caused ‘overheating’ of the non-climate variety. China’s voracious demand for raw materials, in particular, stoked the ‘commodity super-cycle’.[19](#section-53) Easy money also stoked speculation in commodities, touted on Wall Street as a hot ‘alternative asset class’. McKinnon posed a tantalizing counterfactual: ‘If the Arab Spring had been recognized as mainly a food riot, the response of Western governments would have been more measured in taking sides, while focusing more actively on monetary measures to dampen cycles in primary commodity prices.’[20](#section-53)

### THE TAPER TANTRUM

After the financial crisis, borrowers in developing countries took full advantage of the low rates available in the West. Foreign capital poured into the developing world, from Azerbaijan to Zimbabwe. Lending in dollars outside the United States accelerated.[21](#section-53) Western investors also boosted their holdings of local-currency debt issued by emerging markets.[22](#section-53) Countries whose bonds offered the largest carry (i.e. spread over Treasuries) proved popular destinations for yield-starved investors.[23](#section-53) As interest rates within emerging markets were now more closely correlated with US rates, their financial systems became more sensitive to shifts in American monetary policy – in particular, to any appreciation in the dollar.[24](#section-53)

Emerging markets’ economic destiny hinged on decisions taken in the Eccles Building in Washington, the headquarters of the Federal Reserve Board. On 22 May 2013, Ben Bernanke announced to Congress that the Fed intended to gradually taper its ongoing securities purchases. The financial markets threw a fit – or ‘taper tantrum’, as it was dubbed. Cross-border carry trades screeched to a halt. Bond funds, the prime source of foreign lending for many emerging markets, suffered outflows. Sovereign bond auctions failed in South Korea, Russia and Colombia. In China, the ATM machines at one of the large banks ceased issuing cash. Commodity bubbles around the world imploded. The American currency rose abruptly on the foreign exchanges, increasing the burden of all those foreign dollar-denominated debts. Emerging markets had lost the currency wars.

The taper tantrum brought the curtain down on Brazil’s economic miracle. Despite Finance Minister Mantega’s complaints, South America’s largest economy had come roaring back after the financial crisis: Brazilian GDP growth approached 10 per cent (in early 2010) and unemployment fell to an all-time low. Consumer demand expanded so fast that local brewers ran out of beer cans. In September 2010, state oil-producer Petrobras raised $70 billion in the largest share offering in history. Buoyed by capital inflows, the Brazilian real was deemed the ‘world’s most overvalued currency’. The *Wall Street Journal* reported that taxis and Coca-Cola were more expensive in São Paulo than Manhattan.[25](#section-53)

A leading producer of iron ore, soya beans and oil, Brazil was a prime beneficiary of the global commodity boom. No Brazilian benefited more than Eike Batista, a former insurance salesman turned gold miner. Batista put together a large energy and logistics conglomerate, EBX. At one point he boasted that the reserves of his oil company, OGX Petróleo e Gás, were worth $1 trillion. His shipping business, OSX, was busy constructing the largest shipyard in the southern hemisphere. (The X in the names of Batista’s various companies stood for the multiplication of value.) The flamboyant businessman enjoyed the conventional accoutrements of fame and wealth in the twenty-first century: supermodel girlfriends, fast cars, speed boats, private jets and a million adoring followers on Twitter. In 2010, *Forbes* reckoned Batista to be the world’s eighth-richest person.

Batista’s fortunes took a downward turn in 2012, however, when it was revealed that OGX’s oil reserves had been overstated. The collapse in the oil price, coincident with the taper tantrum, provided the death blow to his complex business empire. In October 2013, OGX filed for bankruptcy protection, owing more than $5 billion, including some $3.6 billion in dollar-denominated bonds that were held by some of the world’s top bond funds. Within the space of twelve months, Batista’s personal wealth shrank by $34 billion, earning him the title of the world’s least wealthy person – a ‘minus billionaire’. A New York money manager summed up Batista’s fate: ‘He tried to do too much too fast and he tried to do that with borrowed money.’[26](#section-53)

The trajectory of Brazil’s economy followed that of its most famous businessman. As foreign capital inflows dried up, the currency collapsed. But a cheaper real didn’t prevent the current account deficit from exploding. Soaring inflation forced the Central Bank of Brazil to hike interest rates to over 14 per cent. Cut off from the international capital markets, local companies grappled with their foreign-currency debts and rising interest costs. Ratings agency Fitch reported that most Brazilian firms were in ‘survival mode’.[27](#section-53) The country entered its longest recession since the 1930s, a squeeze so severe that Goldman Sachs feared it might turn into a full-blown depression.

Five years after its record-breaking stock issue, Petrobras shares were languishing, and its bonds had been downgraded to junk. These turned out to be the least of its problems. The Brazilian state oil company now found itself at the centre of a massive corruption scandal, dubbed Operation Car Wash, involving billions of dollars of bribes paid to politicians and government officials. Operation Car Wash led eventually to the imprisonment of former President Lula and the impeachment of his successor, Dilma Rousseff.[28](#section-53) Also entangled in the web of corruption was the hapless Batista, who received a thirty-year prison sentence for bribing officials. (In a subsequent trial, a further eight years were added for insider trading.) The bribery scandal, together with falling oil prices, forced Petrobras to write-down assets to the tune of $17 billion.

Brazil was not the only emerging market to face an epic corruption scandal. In late 2015, it was discovered that billions of dollars had gone missing from Malaysia’s development fund, 1MDB – of which a large chunk reportedly ended up in the bank accounts of the country’s Prime Minister, Najib Razak. Much of the stolen money found its way to the United States, where it was spent on works of art, fancy yachts and luxury properties. Malaysia’s missing funds also financed Martin Scorsese’s film *The Wolf of Wall Street*, which, given the involvement of Goldman Sachs in raising money for 1MDB, was most fitting. Thus, carry-trade dollars that left the United States in search of higher returns abroad returned home, laundered via off-shore financial centres – in Switzerland, the Seychelles, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Panama and elsewhere. The grand theft at Malaysia’s development fund was replicated in less newsworthy fashion by countless emerging-market kleptocrats, their ill-gotten fortunes recycled into prime properties in London, Miami, New York, Sydney and other welcoming destinations.

### THE INTEREST-RATE LOBBY

After Brazil’s fall from grace in 2013, the BRICs turned stone cold. Wall Street now fretted about the ‘Fragile Five’: India, Indonesia, Turkey and South Africa joined Brazil in the emerging markets’ hall of shame. Turkey was pickled in debt after its banks and companies had gorged on foreign capital. Foreign loans fuelled a building boom – a third bridge across the Bosporus, the world’s largest airport under construction, a sprawl of skyscrapers encircling Istanbul and dozens of new shopping malls. Foreign loans filled the gaping hole in Turkey’s current account. Foreign debts accumulated on the balance sheets of Turkish corporations, including record levels of debt denominated in foreign currencies. The foreign liabilities of Turkish banks alone amounted to more than a third of the country’s GDP.[29](#section-53)

Turkey’s Prime Minister Recep Tyyip Erdoǧan had no problem with all this foreign debt. What irked the Turkish autocrat beyond reason was the country’s high and rising interest rates. In the months after the taper tantrum, the lira tanked. A crash in the Turkish stock market and rising bond yields in June 2013 coincided with demonstrations in Istanbul’s Taksim Square, where protesters clashed with riot police.[30](#section-53) The Central Bank of Turkey responded to this crisis with a number of emergency rate increases – raising rates by more than 4.25 percentage points on a single day the following January. ‘Treason,’ exclaimed Erdoǧan, who envisioned a cabal of international speculators – the ‘interest-rate lobby’, he called them – who profited from high interest rates at Turkey’s expense.

Over the following years, Erdoǧan didn’t let up on this obsession. On the eve of a presidential election in May 2018, Erdoǧan (who became President in 2014) identified his main opponent. Interest rates, he declared, were the ‘mother and father of all evil’. The President promised to continue until ‘victory in the fight against this curse of interest rates’.[31](#section-53) By this date, the lira was on the brink of a currency crisis as Turkish corporations struggled with their massive foreign debts. In September 2018, with the currency spiralling downwards and inflation escalating out of control, the central bank hiked its lending rate to 24 per cent. Erdoǧan blamed ‘online fictional currency plots’ for the lira’s collapse.

Yet, if a global ‘interest-rate lobby’ might be said to exist, it was one that campaigned invariably for lower interest rates, and in Turkey the lobby’s chief representative was none other than the President himself. His anti-usury invective belonged to a venerable Islamic tradition but, in this case, it was misdirected. High interest rates hadn’t landed Turkey in trouble. Rather, it was ultra-low interest rates in the United States and Europe that drove foreign lenders to Turkish shores. Domestic monetary policy had also been loose: in the five years after 2008, Turkish lending rates were low in real terms and trailed far below the economy’s growth rate.[32](#section-53) Easy money financed the country’s construction boom and property bubble. Easy money encouraged Turkish corporations to take on too much debt, borrowing in liras and foreign currencies. Easy money fuelled the rising inflation, which peaked at 25 per cent in 2018.

As the tenth anniversary of Lehman’s bankruptcy approached, Turkey’s real estate market resembled Spain’s on the eve of the global financial crisis. What a leading Istanbul estate agent called a ‘big Ponzi scheme’ was broken. Residential developments ground to a halt, as Turkey’s housing market was weighed down with a couple of million unsold houses. One incomplete development, the Brooklyn Dream project on the Asian side of Istanbul, had been marketed to ‘those who want an active and dreamlike life in the center of the city’. But the developer ran out of cash and local residents, who’d been promised new apartments, were found to be inhabiting tents on the building site where their demolished homes had stood.[33](#section-53) A living nightmare.

Turkey’s financial woes were shared to some degree or other across emerging markets. A decade of ultra-low interest rates in the developed world had saddled developing countries with too much debt: between 2008 and 2018, their non-financial debt climbed from 107 per cent to 192 per cent of GDP.[34](#section-53) An increasing proportion of these liabilities were owed to foreigners.[35](#section-53) Foreign dollar loans exceeded $11 trillion (in 2016), of which nearly $4 trillion was owed by emerging markets – around twice as much as a few years earlier.[36](#section-53) Much of this borrowing was poorly invested and generated little by way of economic growth, or was used for financial engineering as companies in emerging markets borrowed in dollars and lent onwards in their domestic markets at higher yields.

### AN END TO GLOBALIZATION?

A feedback loop exists between globalization and interest rates: more trade between countries tends to reduce inflation pressures and weaken the bargaining power of labour, both of which have an impact on the level of interest rates. The first wave of globalization, which dates from the 1860s to the end of the century, was accompanied by mild deflation and falling long-term interest rates.[fn4](#section-58) During the recent globalization phase, from 1980 onwards, China and other developing countries grabbed an increased share of world trade. Traded goods’ prices declined and millions of manufacturing jobs were ‘off-shored’ to emerging markets. Thus, globalization reduced both inflation and wage growth, which, in turn, allowed Western central banks to reduce interest rates, thereby spurring the greatest bull market in bonds in history.

Yet the decline in interest rates also propelled globalization. Since international trade credit is mostly denominated in dollars, when the cost of borrowing in dollars falls multinational companies are inclined to construct longer supply chains. In the era of easy money, global manufacturing took place across several continents and multiple countries (six on average). For instance, car engines built in Japan were shipped to Canada for further work, fitted into vehicle chassis in Mexico, with the finished cars sold in the United States. Lengthier supply chains tied up vast amounts of working capital and required ample financing.[37](#section-53) Manufacturers in emerging markets benefited most from the lengthening of supply chains.

Economists at the BIS suggested that the rapid expansion of world trade at the turn of the century might have been ‘a bubble, made possible by ample global liquidity’.[38](#section-53) Like all bubbles, the global trade ‘bubble’ was inherently fragile. Over-extended supply chains require accommodative monetary conditions. Political support is equally important, although often overlooked. In the United States, the loss of manufacturing jobs to China eventually provoked a backlash against globalization.[fn5](#section-58) Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign promise to bring manufacturing jobs home helped to take him to the White House.

The collapse of international trade in the 1930s is commonly attributed to the protectionist US tariffs imposed by the Smoot–Hawley Act of 1930. But tariffs were only part of the story. The financial side deserves greater emphasis. During the 1920s, dollars flowed out of the United States attracted by the higher interest rates on offer in Central Europe and South America. Large international capital movements were facilitated by the Gold Exchange Standard. It was the hike in US interest rates in 1928 which halted America’s foreign lending and inaugurated the global economic downturn.

Cut off from the capital markets, the Austrian bank Creditanstalt was the first domino to fall. After Creditanstalt’s collapse in 1930 the free movement of international capital came to an end, to be replaced by exchange controls, ‘blocked currencies’ and ‘standstill agreements’ on defaulted foreign debts. International trade withered. Once tariffs were in place, international trade was organized on a bilateral basis between countries. Economic nationalism attracted some surprising new advocates: ‘let goods be homespun,’ wrote the great liberal Keynes in 1933, ‘and above all, let finance be primarily national.’[39](#section-53)

Can it happen again? A decade after the financial crisis, President Trump was fighting trade wars with China and America’s erstwhile ally the European Union. At the same time, Britain’s decision to leave the European Union threatened the free movement of goods and services across Europe. After 2008, capital controls were introduced on several occasions in Europe (in Iceland, Cyprus and Greece) and a number of emerging markets (Azerbaijan, Egypt, Nigeria and Turkmenistan). Beijing strengthened its own capital controls, making it more difficult for foreign multinationals to repatriate profits, and for its own firms and citizens to take money out of the People’s Republic. After capital flight from emerging markets took off in 2015, the head of Mexico’s central bank suggested it was time for them to ‘become unconventional’.

The ‘Achilles heel’ of the international monetary system, according to the BIS’s Claudio Borio, was its ‘persistent expansionary bias’. This state of affairs wasn’t healthy for Americans, since foreigners’ limitless appetite for dollars pushed the United States ever more into hock to the rest of the world.[fn6](#section-58) Nor was it healthy for foreigners. The ‘persistent expansionary bias’ resulted in the continuous accumulation of global financial imbalances. The prolonged period of ultra-low rates stretched the elasticity of the international monetary system, as countries accumulated large foreign liabilities – in particular, debt denominated in US dollars.

The elasticity of the Dollar Standard isn’t its only problem. As we have seen, American monetary policy has an inordinate influence abroad. The Fed doesn’t formally consider the impact of its actions on foreign countries but sticks to its mandates of controlling inflation and delivering low domestic unemployment. America’s central bank exercises power without responsibility. As President Nixon’s Treasury Secretary, John Connally, famously told foreign finance ministers in 1971, ‘the dollar is our currency, but your problem.’ In similar vein, Fed Chairman Bernanke shrugged off foreign complaints about currency wars in 2011, claiming that ‘countries with sound monetary, budget and trade policies could better withstand any short term disruptions from our easing.’[40](#section-53) Several years later Chairman Jerome Powell denied that the Fed and other Western central banks were responsible for the surge in foreign capital flows into emerging markets.[41](#section-53)

Neither of these claims bears scrutiny. As Borio writes, ‘The interaction of monetary regimes spreads easy monetary conditions from core economies to the rest of the world and hence heightens the risk of build-up of financial imbalances.’[42](#section-53) The Fed’s policy of easy money and quantitative easing produced what were euphemistically called ‘spillover effects’ across emerging markets. Outbreaks of global financial turbulence from the taper tantrum of 2013 onwards coincided with monetary tightening in the United States. The Fed funds rate reached 2 per cent in 2018, an extremely low level by historic standards but sufficient to induce currency crises in Argentina and Turkey.

Just as financial stability seeds instability in domestic markets, so it does on the foreign exchanges. As Borio’s colleague Hyun Song Shin warned, ‘the longer policy dampens instability, the larger the risk of a snapback.’[43](#section-53) The increasing vulnerability of emerging markets to US monetary policy provided yet another reason, if one were needed, for the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates low. Over time, the crises of the Dollar Standard have become both more costly and geographically more widespread. This is a worrying trend. Borio suggested (in 2014) that the international monetary and financial system was in urgent need of reform:

> The risks of failing to implement the necessary policy adjustments should not be underestimated. They include entrenching instability in the global system, returning to the modern equivalent of the divisive competitive devaluations of the interwar years and, ultimately, triggering *an epoch-defining seismic rupture* in policy regimes, back to an era of trade and financial protectionism and, possibly, stagnation combined with inflation.[44](#section-53)

Maverick tech billionaire Peter Thiel added a sobering thought: all great historic bubbles, from the Mississippi Bubble to the current day, had coincided with advances in globalization. The previous quarter of a century had produced a string of bubbles and busts that ‘represent[ed] different facets of a single Great Boom of unprecedented size and duration’. Either globalization would succeed, said Thiel, ‘or it is the final and greatest bubble in history’.[45](#section-53)

<!-- rl-section id="sec-chapter017" class="titlepage" title="17" -->

## The Mother and Father of All Evil

> *The dollar is our currency but your problem.*
>
> US Treasury Secretary John Connally, 1971

### THE DOLLAR STANDARD

Interest rates have always regulated international capital flows. In the era of the Gold Standard, this job was done automatically. If the Bank of England brought rates much below foreign levels, gold would leave its vaults for foreign shores. ‘Loanable capital, like every other commodity, comes where there is most to be made of it,’ wrote Bagehot of Victorian lending practices. In order to attract gold back to the City of London, the Bank of England would have had to raise its lending rate. After the Bretton Woods system collapsed in 1971, the US dollar became the global reserve currency. After this date most international trade was denominated in the US currency, along with a large share of cross-border financial transactions. Dozens of countries pegged their own currencies to the dollar.

If the Gold Standard was characterized by its ‘golden fetters’, the chief vice of the Dollar Standard is its extreme elasticity. Central bank reserves are mostly composed of dollar-denominated securities (US Treasury bonds and agency debt), which, unlike gold, can be issued without limit. As the keeper of the world’s reserve currency, the United States doesn’t need to maintain its own foreign-exchange reserves, nor worry about its balance of payments. There is no limit on how many dollars flow abroad nor how much the United States borrows from foreigners. America can run what Jacques Rueff called ‘deficits without tears’, and over the years it has taken advantage of this exorbitant privilege to become the world’s largest international debtor.

US interest rates aren’t influenced by international capital flows. Absent the prospect of inflation, there is no limit on how low interest rates can sink. (The question of whether the Fed could set negative rates is murky from a legal perspective.) Not everything has changed, however. Differentials in interest rates between countries still influence the amount and direction of cross-border lending. The most important interest-rate spread is that between the cost of borrowing in the United States and elsewhere. Countries that peg their currencies to the dollar are obliged to shadow American monetary policy: they must loosen when the Fed loosens and tighten when the Fed tightens. When the US central bank eases, dollar-peggers often intervene in the foreign exchanges: to prevent their currencies from appreciating, their central banks buy dollars with freshly printed local currency, thereby further loosening domestic monetary conditions.

In short, when the United States adopts easy money it unleashes a ‘global monetary plague’.[1](#section-53) The plague is not contained to countries which peg to the dollar: even those with floating currencies are infected. When US interest rates fall below foreign rates, international carry trades take off. Investors borrow dollars and invest the proceeds abroad at higher yields. Foreigners are also encouraged to take out cheap dollar-denominated loans. (The yen and euro are also commonly used to finance cross-border carry trades.) For instance, when Iceland’s economy overheated in the early 2000s its central bank raised rates. But high Icelandic rates attracted hordes of carry traders who borrowed in foreign currencies (dollars, euros and yen) to acquire krona-denominated securities, known as ‘glacier bonds’, and lent directly to Icelandic banks, thereby easing, rather than tightening, monetary conditions.[2](#section-53)

### THE FIRST PHASE OF GLOBAL LIQUIDITY

The early years of this century witnessed a remarkable growth in central bank reserves. Conventional wisdom maintains that the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves indicated a ‘global savings glut’. Emerging markets were said to be amassing reserves in order to protect themselves against another Asian-style crisis. But the link between the growth of foreign exchange reserves and ‘excess savings’ (i.e., current account surpluses) is tenuous.[3](#section-53) Several countries, including Turkey, expanded their foreign reserves while running current account deficits. Some economists, including John Taylor of Stanford, found no evidence that the global savings rate had actually increased.

An alternative account holds that the world in the early years of the new millennium was suffering a surfeit of finance – a ‘global banking glut’.[4](#section-53) According to this interpretation, the Greenspan Fed’s easy money stimulated a rise in cross-border capital flows, which increased threefold in the first years of the century.[5](#section-53) This explosion of international lending fuelled a global credit bubble.[6](#section-53) Countries which operated a dollar peg responded to the surge in capital inflows by acquiring the incoming dollars. Hence, the extraordinary increase in foreign exchange reserves.

As the world’s reserve currency, the US dollar served as the main funding currency for international carry trades. European banks borrowed in the New York money markets to acquire subprime securities. Europe had its own carry trades. Cross-border bank loans financed Greece’s enormous current account deficit and real estate booms in Spain and Ireland.[7](#section-53) Foreign lending to Central Europe topped $1 trillion in 2007, enabling Romanian credit to grow at an annualized rate of 66 per cent, financing a Latvian current account deficit to the tune of a quarter of GDP, and allowing Poles and Hungarians to take out cheap mortgages, denominated in euros and Swiss francs.[8](#section-53) By the onset of the global financial crisis, Iceland’s foreign debts had grown to nearly nine times its national output.[fn1](#section-58)

### THE SECOND PHASE OF GLOBAL LIQUIDITY

The financial convulsions of 2007–8 may have been triggered by losses on American subprime mortgages, but it’s more accurate to describe the global crisis as a ‘giant carry trade gone wrong’.[fn2](#section-58) After Lehman’s bankruptcy, foreign banks which had borrowed dollars to buy US mortgage securities lost access to the international money markets. The Federal Reserve came to their rescue, providing massive lines of dollar credit to central banks in Europe and Asia. Chairman Bernanke’s prompt actions prevented a collapse of the global monetary system, as had occurred in the early 1930s.[9](#section-53)

But this very success, combined with the move to zero interest rates at the core of the global financial system, revived the international carry trade. Economist Hyun Song Shin of the BIS coined the term the ‘second phase of global liquidity’ to describe the resurgence of international capital flows after 2008. Both phases of global liquidity were characterized by abnormally low interest rates in the United States, low levels of market volatility (as measured by the VIX) and extensive cross-border lending.[10](#section-53) In the first phase, international capital flows financed credit booms and real estate bubbles on the edges of Europe. In the second phase, foreign capital mostly poured into emerging markets. In the first phase, the financial systems on the periphery of Europe became dangerously exposed. In the second phase, financial weakness spread throughout the developing world.

The second phase of global liquidity got off to an explosive start. Over the course of 2009, emerging market bond funds witnessed record inflows.[11](#section-53) The IMF observed in November that the dollar was ‘now serving as the funding currency for carry trades’.[12](#section-53) New York University economist Nouriel Roubini issued a starker warning. The combination of easy money, quantitative easing and a weakening dollar had produced the ‘mother of all carry trades’, said Roubini:

> But one day this bubble will burst, leading to the biggest coordinated asset bust ever … the longer and bigger the carry trades and the larger the asset bubble, the bigger will be the ensuing asset bubble crash. The Fed and other policymakers seem unaware of the monster bubble they are creating. The longer they remain blind, the harder the markets will fall.[13](#section-53)

Of more immediate concern to policymakers in emerging markets was the rapid appreciation of their currencies, induced by a weak dollar and unconstrained capital inflows. Brazil’s Finance Minister Guido Mantega complained that the United States was engaged in a currency war. To discourage hot money flows, Mantega announced a tax on foreign purchases of Brazilian stocks and bonds. Central banks in the developing world played a defensive role in the currency wars, intervening in the currency markets to buy dollars. In the process they added greatly to their foreign exchange reserves. By 2013 global foreign exchange reserves were touching $12 trillion, up from $2 trillion at the turn of the century. (Since trade imbalances were shrinking, there was now less talk of any global savings glut.)

Massive purchases of dollar securities by central banks put downward pressure on US Treasury yields. Foreign exchange interventions by central banks, combined with hot money flows and increased lending by state banks (notably in China, India and Brazil), eased credit conditions across the emerging markets; as did the fact that their domestic interest rates were falling, drawn downwards by the gravitational pull of zero interest rates at the heart of the world’s financial system.[14](#section-53) Inflation started to pick up across the emerging markets. By early 2010, the BRICs – Goldman Sachs’ catchy acronym for Brazil, Russia, India and China – were overheating.[15](#section-53) In October, rubber and cotton futures jumped to record levels. Arabica coffee prices hit a thirteen-year high. Flooding across South East Asia affected the rice harvest, driving up rice futures by more than 50 per cent.[16](#section-53)

### THE ARAB SPRING

On 17 December 2010, a young Tunisian street vendor doused his clothes with petrol and set himself alight outside the Governor’s office in the provincial town of Sidi Bouzid. Mohamed Bouazizi committed suicide in protest against the actions of local police who had confiscated his wares and smashed his cart. The day after his death riots broke out in Sidi Bouzid. Unrest spread rapidly across North Africa and the Middle East. Within a month Tunisian President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali had been forced from office, followed soon after by the departure of Libya’s Colonel Gaddafi and Egypt’s Hosni Mubarak.

Like many popular uprisings in history, the Arab Spring started out as a bread riot.[17](#section-53) Over the course of the year, world cereal prices climbed by 29 per cent.[18](#section-53) Bouazizi earned his pittance selling vegetables, which might explain why corrupt officials were keen to appropriate his wares. North Africa, once the grain basket of the Roman Empire, was now the world’s largest food importer. Half of Egypt’s wheat – the main staple for the country’s 80 million-odd population – came from abroad. A much-photographed protester in Cairo’s Tahrir Square wore a ‘bread helmet’ made from a croissant and two bread sticks held together with cling film. Commentators blamed crop failures among the world’s leading food exporters on climate change.

But some other factor must have contributed to the sharp rise in food prices, since the price of industrial commodities, whose supply was unaffected by the weather, also soared in the months prior to the Arab Spring. Most industrial commodities, and precious metals from copper to silver, were trading at bubble levels.[fn3](#section-58) That additional factor was the Federal Reserve’s monetary policies. Stanford economist Ronald McKinnon argued that the Arab Spring originated with ultra-low interest rates in the United States, which, as we have seen, drove capital flows into the emerging world and caused ‘overheating’ of the non-climate variety. China’s voracious demand for raw materials, in particular, stoked the ‘commodity super-cycle’.[19](#section-53) Easy money also stoked speculation in commodities, touted on Wall Street as a hot ‘alternative asset class’. McKinnon posed a tantalizing counterfactual: ‘If the Arab Spring had been recognized as mainly a food riot, the response of Western governments would have been more measured in taking sides, while focusing more actively on monetary measures to dampen cycles in primary commodity prices.’[20](#section-53)

### THE TAPER TANTRUM

After the financial crisis, borrowers in developing countries took full advantage of the low rates available in the West. Foreign capital poured into the developing world, from Azerbaijan to Zimbabwe. Lending in dollars outside the United States accelerated.[21](#section-53) Western investors also boosted their holdings of local-currency debt issued by emerging markets.[22](#section-53) Countries whose bonds offered the largest carry (i.e. spread over Treasuries) proved popular destinations for yield-starved investors.[23](#section-53) As interest rates within emerging markets were now more closely correlated with US rates, their financial systems became more sensitive to shifts in American monetary policy – in particular, to any appreciation in the dollar.[24](#section-53)

Emerging markets’ economic destiny hinged on decisions taken in the Eccles Building in Washington, the headquarters of the Federal Reserve Board. On 22 May 2013, Ben Bernanke announced to Congress that the Fed intended to gradually taper its ongoing securities purchases. The financial markets threw a fit – or ‘taper tantrum’, as it was dubbed. Cross-border carry trades screeched to a halt. Bond funds, the prime source of foreign lending for many emerging markets, suffered outflows. Sovereign bond auctions failed in South Korea, Russia and Colombia. In China, the ATM machines at one of the large banks ceased issuing cash. Commodity bubbles around the world imploded. The American currency rose abruptly on the foreign exchanges, increasing the burden of all those foreign dollar-denominated debts. Emerging markets had lost the currency wars.

The taper tantrum brought the curtain down on Brazil’s economic miracle. Despite Finance Minister Mantega’s complaints, South America’s largest economy had come roaring back after the financial crisis: Brazilian GDP growth approached 10 per cent (in early 2010) and unemployment fell to an all-time low. Consumer demand expanded so fast that local brewers ran out of beer cans. In September 2010, state oil-producer Petrobras raised $70 billion in the largest share offering in history. Buoyed by capital inflows, the Brazilian real was deemed the ‘world’s most overvalued currency’. The *Wall Street Journal* reported that taxis and Coca-Cola were more expensive in São Paulo than Manhattan.[25](#section-53)

A leading producer of iron ore, soya beans and oil, Brazil was a prime beneficiary of the global commodity boom. No Brazilian benefited more than Eike Batista, a former insurance salesman turned gold miner. Batista put together a large energy and logistics conglomerate, EBX. At one point he boasted that the reserves of his oil company, OGX Petróleo e Gás, were worth $1 trillion. His shipping business, OSX, was busy constructing the largest shipyard in the southern hemisphere. (The X in the names of Batista’s various companies stood for the multiplication of value.) The flamboyant businessman enjoyed the conventional accoutrements of fame and wealth in the twenty-first century: supermodel girlfriends, fast cars, speed boats, private jets and a million adoring followers on Twitter. In 2010, *Forbes* reckoned Batista to be the world’s eighth-richest person.

Batista’s fortunes took a downward turn in 2012, however, when it was revealed that OGX’s oil reserves had been overstated. The collapse in the oil price, coincident with the taper tantrum, provided the death blow to his complex business empire. In October 2013, OGX filed for bankruptcy protection, owing more than $5 billion, including some $3.6 billion in dollar-denominated bonds that were held by some of the world’s top bond funds. Within the space of twelve months, Batista’s personal wealth shrank by $34 billion, earning him the title of the world’s least wealthy person – a ‘minus billionaire’. A New York money manager summed up Batista’s fate: ‘He tried to do too much too fast and he tried to do that with borrowed money.’[26](#section-53)

The trajectory of Brazil’s economy followed that of its most famous businessman. As foreign capital inflows dried up, the currency collapsed. But a cheaper real didn’t prevent the current account deficit from exploding. Soaring inflation forced the Central Bank of Brazil to hike interest rates to over 14 per cent. Cut off from the international capital markets, local companies grappled with their foreign-currency debts and rising interest costs. Ratings agency Fitch reported that most Brazilian firms were in ‘survival mode’.[27](#section-53) The country entered its longest recession since the 1930s, a squeeze so severe that Goldman Sachs feared it might turn into a full-blown depression.

Five years after its record-breaking stock issue, Petrobras shares were languishing, and its bonds had been downgraded to junk. These turned out to be the least of its problems. The Brazilian state oil company now found itself at the centre of a massive corruption scandal, dubbed Operation Car Wash, involving billions of dollars of bribes paid to politicians and government officials. Operation Car Wash led eventually to the imprisonment of former President Lula and the impeachment of his successor, Dilma Rousseff.[28](#section-53) Also entangled in the web of corruption was the hapless Batista, who received a thirty-year prison sentence for bribing officials. (In a subsequent trial, a further eight years were added for insider trading.) The bribery scandal, together with falling oil prices, forced Petrobras to write-down assets to the tune of $17 billion.

Brazil was not the only emerging market to face an epic corruption scandal. In late 2015, it was discovered that billions of dollars had gone missing from Malaysia’s development fund, 1MDB – of which a large chunk reportedly ended up in the bank accounts of the country’s Prime Minister, Najib Razak. Much of the stolen money found its way to the United States, where it was spent on works of art, fancy yachts and luxury properties. Malaysia’s missing funds also financed Martin Scorsese’s film *The Wolf of Wall Street*, which, given the involvement of Goldman Sachs in raising money for 1MDB, was most fitting. Thus, carry-trade dollars that left the United States in search of higher returns abroad returned home, laundered via off-shore financial centres – in Switzerland, the Seychelles, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Panama and elsewhere. The grand theft at Malaysia’s development fund was replicated in less newsworthy fashion by countless emerging-market kleptocrats, their ill-gotten fortunes recycled into prime properties in London, Miami, New York, Sydney and other welcoming destinations.

### THE INTEREST-RATE LOBBY

After Brazil’s fall from grace in 2013, the BRICs turned stone cold. Wall Street now fretted about the ‘Fragile Five’: India, Indonesia, Turkey and South Africa joined Brazil in the emerging markets’ hall of shame. Turkey was pickled in debt after its banks and companies had gorged on foreign capital. Foreign loans fuelled a building boom – a third bridge across the Bosporus, the world’s largest airport under construction, a sprawl of skyscrapers encircling Istanbul and dozens of new shopping malls. Foreign loans filled the gaping hole in Turkey’s current account. Foreign debts accumulated on the balance sheets of Turkish corporations, including record levels of debt denominated in foreign currencies. The foreign liabilities of Turkish banks alone amounted to more than a third of the country’s GDP.[29](#section-53)

Turkey’s Prime Minister Recep Tyyip Erdoǧan had no problem with all this foreign debt. What irked the Turkish autocrat beyond reason was the country’s high and rising interest rates. In the months after the taper tantrum, the lira tanked. What a leading Istanbul estate agent called a ‘big Ponzi scheme’ was broken. Residential developments ground to a halt, as Turkey’s housing market was weighed down with a couple of million unsold houses. But the developer ran out of cash and local residents, who’d been promised new apartments, were found to be inhabiting tents on the building site where their demolished homes had stood.[33](#section-53) A living nightmare.

Thus, globalization reduced both inflation and wage growth, which, in turn, allowed Western central banks to reduce interest rates, thereby spurring the greatest bull market in bonds in history.

Yet the decline in interest rates also propelled globalization. Since international trade credit is mostly denominated in dollars, when the cost of borrowing in dollars falls multinational companies are inclined to construct longer supply chains. In the era of easy money, global manufacturing took place across several continents and multiple countries (six on average). For instance, car engines built in Japan were shipped to Canada for further work, fitted into vehicle chassis in Mexico, with the finished cars sold in the United States. Lengthier supply chains tied up vast amounts of working capital and required ample financing.[37](#section-53) Manufacturers in emerging markets benefited most from the lengthening of supply chains.

Economists at the BIS suggested that the rapid expansion of world trade at the turn of the century might have been ‘a bubble, made possible by ample global liquidity’.[38](#section-53) Like all bubbles, the global trade ‘bubble’ was inherently fragile. Over-extended supply chains require accommodative monetary conditions. Political support is equally important, although often overlooked. In the United States, the loss of manufacturing jobs to China eventually provoked a backlash against globalization.[fn5](#section-58) Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign promise to bring manufacturing jobs home helped to take him to the White House.

The collapse of international trade in the 1930s is commonly attributed to the protectionist US tariffs imposed by the Smoot–Hawley Act of 1930. But tariffs were only part of the story. The financial side deserves greater emphasis. During the 1920s, dollars flowed out of the United States attracted by the higher interest rates on offer in Central Europe and South America. Large international capital movements were facilitated by the Gold Exchange Standard. It was the hike in US interest rates in 1928 which halted America’s foreign lending and inaugurated the global economic downturn.

Cut off from the capital markets, the Austrian bank Creditanstalt was the first domino to fall. After Creditanstalt’s collapse in 1930 the free movement of international capital came to an end, to be replaced by exchange controls, ‘blocked currencies’ and ‘standstill agreements’ on defaulted foreign debts. International trade withered. Once tariffs were in place, international trade was organized on a bilateral basis between countries. Economic nationalism attracted some surprising new advocates: ‘let goods be homespun,’ wrote the great liberal Keynes in 1933, ‘and above all, let finance be primarily national.’[39](#section-53)

Can it happen again? A decade after the financial crisis, President Trump was fighting trade wars with China and America’s erstwhile ally the European Union. At the same time, Britain’s decision to leave the European Union threatened the free movement of goods and services across Europe. After 2008, capital controls were introduced on several occasions in Europe (in Iceland, Cyprus and Greece) and a number of emerging markets (Azerbaijan, Egypt, Nigeria and Turkmenistan). Beijing strengthened its own capital controls, making it more difficult for foreign multinationals to repatriate profits, and for its own firms and citizens to take money out of the People’s Republic. After capital flight from emerging markets took off in 2015, the head of Mexico’s central bank suggested it was time for them to ‘become unconventional’.

The ‘Achilles heel’ of the international monetary system, according to the BIS’s Claudio Borio, was its ‘persistent expansionary bias’. This state of affairs wasn’t healthy for Americans, since foreigners’ limitless appetite for dollars pushed the United States ever more into hock to the rest of the world.[fn6](#section-58) Nor was it healthy for foreigners. The ‘persistent expansionary bias’ resulted in the continuous accumulation of global financial imbalances. The prolonged period of ultra-low rates stretched the elasticity of the international monetary system, as countries accumulated large foreign liabilities – in particular, debt denominated in US dollars.

The elasticity of the Dollar Standard isn’t its only problem. As we have seen, American monetary policy has an inordinate influence abroad. The Fed doesn’t formally consider the impact of its actions on foreign countries but sticks to its mandates of controlling inflation and delivering low domestic unemployment. America’s central bank exercises power without responsibility. As President Nixon’s Treasury Secretary, John Connally, famously told foreign finance ministers in 1971, ‘the dollar is our currency, but your problem.’ In similar vein, Fed Chairman Bernanke shrugged off foreign complaints about currency wars in 2011, claiming that ‘countries with sound monetary, budget and trade policies could better withstand any short term disruptions from our easing.’[40](#section-53) Several years later Chairman Jerome Powell denied that the Fed and other Western central banks were responsible for the surge in foreign capital flows into emerging markets.[41](#section-53)

Neither of these claims bears scrutiny. As Borio writes, ‘The interaction of monetary regimes spreads easy monetary conditions from core economies to the rest of the world and hence heightens the risk of build-up of financial imbalances.’[42](#section-53) The Fed’s policy of easy money and quantitative easing produced what were euphemistically called ‘spillover effects’ across emerging markets. Outbreaks of global financial turbulence from the taper tantrum of 2013 onwards coincided with monetary tightening in the United States. The Fed funds rate reached 2 per cent in 2018, an extremely low level by historic standards but sufficient to induce currency crises in Argentina and Turkey.

Just as financial stability seeds instability in domestic markets, so it does on the foreign exchanges. As Borio’s colleague Hyun Song Shin warned, ‘the longer policy dampens instability, the larger the risk of a snapback.’[43](#section-53) The increasing vulnerability of emerging markets to US monetary policy provided yet another reason, if one were needed, for the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates low. Over time, the crises of the Dollar Standard have become both more costly and geographically more widespread. This is a worrying trend. Borio suggested (in 2014) that the international monetary and financial system was in urgent need of reform:

> The risks of failing to implement the necessary policy adjustments should not be underestimated. They include entrenching instability in the global system, returning to the modern equivalent of the divisive competitive devaluations of the interwar years and, ultimately, triggering *an epoch-defining seismic rupture* in policy regimes, back to an era of trade and financial protectionism and, possibly, stagnation combined with inflation.[44](#section-53)

Maverick tech billionaire Peter Thiel added a sobering thought: all great historic bubbles, from the Mississippi Bubble to the current day, had coincided with advances in globalization. The previous quarter of a century had produced a string of bubbles and busts that ‘represent[ed] different facets of a single Great Boom of unprecedented size and duration’. Either globalization would succeed, said Thiel, ‘or it is the final and greatest bubble in history’.[45](#section-53)

<!-- rl-section id="section-32" class="epub-section" kicker="Section 32" title="18" -->

## 18

## Financial Repression with Chinese Characteristics

> *[T]he biggest problem with China’s economy is that the growth is unstable, unbalanced, uncoordinated and unsustainable.*
>
> Premier Wen Jiabao, 2007

Successful economic development requires that credit be allocated efficiently. That job is ill done when the state retains control over the banking system and when interest rates are set at inappropriate levels. In the early 1970s, Stanford economist Ronald McKinnon coined the pejorative term ‘financial repression’ to describe the negative consequences of keeping interest rates below the level of inflation. Under such circumstances, borrowers benefit at the expense of savers. Market forces no longer determine how credit is dispensed. Banks become risk averse, preferring to lend to large corporations and state-related entities. Savers look to protect their wealth from inflation by investing in real estate or taking their money abroad. In short, financial repression stifles economic development and weakens the financial system.[1](#section-53)

Financial repression might be said to have been invented in China. The tradition of controlling interest rates dates back as far as the Han period at the beginning of the Common Era.[2](#section-53) The Tang capped interest charged by private lenders while lending their own money at higher rates through the offices of ‘money-catching clerks’.[3](#section-53) Under the Song, guilds were forced to lend to the government at below market rates. The Mongols lent at very favourable rates to Uighur merchants, who ‘used the funds in money lending and various other business enterprises, including foreign trade’. China’s first state bonds were issued only in the late nineteenth century and even then some officials questioned whether the Emperor should have to pay interest.[fn1](#section-58)

Given the insecurity of commerce and the immaturity of financial development in the Middle Kingdom, ‘land purchase was the only method of investment.’[4](#section-53) Loans secured by property attracted the lowest interest. This attitude is summed up in Chang Ying’s *Remarks on a Regular Livelihood*, written in the early Qing period:

> I have seen much of this world. Pawnbroking, trade, and lending at compound interest are such that one inevitably comes to ruin before long. Even if at first you quickly make rich profits, it is certain to come to nothing in the end. Only land and houses can be for long relied upon.[5](#section-53)

Although paper money was invented in China, the verdict of most historians on the country’s monetary history is damning: ‘from having begun as a brilliant solution to a shortage of copper cash, paper money gradually turned into a bureaucratic monstrosity that hampered the productive forces whose growth it had originally done much to foster.’[6](#section-53) Financial repression served as a tool of political repression.[fn2](#section-58) In his brilliant account of Lord Marcartney’s embassy to the Court of Qianlong, Alain Peyrefitte comments that ‘the exploitation of poverty by usurers was all China knew of capitalism. Even this, however, was not really capitalism, but its opposite: money was made not to be invested but to be spent.’[7](#section-53)

### THE REFORM ERA

In 1974, when Deng Xiaoping led a delegation of officials to a special session of the United Nations in New York, there was scarcely enough foreign currency in the whole of China to finance the trip: the sum total of foreign currency that could be located in Beijing’s banks was just $38,000.[8](#section-53) At the time, the People’s Bank of China was a branch of the Ministry of Finance. Yet by 2010 the People’s Republic had transformed into a financial superpower. Its central bank sat on the world’s largest pile of foreign exchange reserves. The China Development Bank, one of several policy banks, was the world’s largest bank by assets. Two publicly listed Chinese banks were ranked among the top ten most valuable companies.[9](#section-53) Outstanding bank loans exceeded China’s GDP.[10](#section-53)

The period of rapid economic growth commenced with Deng’s economic reforms, launched in the late 1970s. Financial deepening – defined as the accumulation of financial assets faster than non-financial wealth – played an important role in what has been called the China miracle.[11](#section-53) World Bank economists Robert King and Ross Levine find a strong relationship between the expansion of the financial sector and subsequent income growth. Their research suggests that finance leads growth, rather than the other way around. As King and Levine write, ‘When countries have relatively high levels of financial development, economic growth tends to be relatively fast over the next 10 to 30 years.’[12](#section-53)

China’s blistering economic growth in the decades after 1980 appeared to support this finding. By the time of the global financial crisis, however, its economy was beset by a number of severe imbalances – asset price bubbles and credit booms, excess savings and wasteful investments. These imbalances were the product of financial repression, according to McKinnon. In a 2012 paper written shortly before his death, McKinnon suggested that negative real interest rates on Chinese bank deposits had reduced household income. Benchmark rates kept below the market-clearing rate were creating an excessive demand for credit, he added.

State-owned enterprises, which received preferential access to credit, were crowding out private businesses, McKinnon suggested. Low interest rates had boosted investment, but the general quality of lending was poor. Furthermore, savings were moving out of banks into an opaque shadow banking system.[13](#section-53) Financial repression had tilted China’s economy away from consumption towards low-quality investment and fostered asset price bubbles. If *financial deepening* made the China miracle, *financial repression* threatened to undo it.

### HOW FINANCIAL REPRESSION WORKS

Here’s how financial repression was implemented in China. Capital controls trapped savings within the country. Households had little choice but to deposit their savings at one of the large banks. The ‘Big Four’ banks were majority owned and tightly controlled by the state. The central bank set the deposit rate below China’s rate of economic growth, and often below the rate of inflation. Banks lent to state enterprises at below market rates. Since the deposit rate was fixed even lower, the banks were guaranteed fat profits. Government-controlled corporations used the cheap credit they received for investment, often favouring sectors selected by Beijing’s economic planners. Banks and state enterprises were the main beneficiaries of financial repression; household savers were the big losers.

The state control of money and interest and the distribution of cheap credit to favoured parties belong to a venerable Chinese tradition. In Deng’s reform era, however, Beijing copied directly from its Asian neighbours. The Asian economic development model, which relied on driving up exports and large-scale investment, had helped the region’s backward economies catch up with their Western competitors.[14](#section-53) In the 1960s South Korea’s government under General Park Chung-hee used state banks to provide loans at negative real interest rates to exporters and favoured industrial projects.[15](#section-53) China adopted the South Korean template.

Financial repression became firmly established towards the end of the 1990s. At the start of the decade, the People’s Bank applied high interest rates to squeeze inflation out of the system. The currency was devalued in early 1994 and later pegged at a significantly undervalued level to the US dollar. To prevent the yuan from appreciating too rapidly, which would have hurt Chinese exports, the People’s Bank intervened in the foreign exchange markets to sell yuan and buy dollars. The dollar securities acquired in this manner were added to the country’s foreign exchange reserves. Thus, China found itself lending indirectly to American consumers for them to buy its exports. Its massive purchases of American securities put downward pressure on US long-term interest rates.

Joining the Dollar Bloc suited Beijing’s mercantilist inclinations. In December 2001, China became a member of the World Trade Organization. This move coincided with the inception of Alan Greenspan’s easy money policy. The People’s Bank kept interest rates low to maintain the dollar peg. Financial repression emerged as a ‘consequence of the government’s policy of maintaining an undervalued exchange rate’.[16](#section-53) Exports and export-driven investment became the main contributors to China’s economic miracle. In the six years after joining the WTO, exports compounded at a mindboggling annual rate of 30 per cent. In 2007, China overtook the United States to become the world’s top exporter.[17](#section-53) Foreign capital poured into the country, driven by expectations that the yuan would appreciate. China’s low interest rates were partly intended to discourage these hot money flows.[18](#section-53)

Much of the new money created by the central bank’s foreign exchange interventions ended up as deposits in Chinese banks, further easing monetary conditions.[19](#section-53) Another consequence of the dollar peg was that domestic monetary policy was increasingly influenced by the decisions taken by the Federal Reserve. The People’s Bank was commonly believed to target a 2.5 percentage point spread above the Fed funds rate.[20](#section-53) A month after the Fed lowered its rate to 1.5 per cent in January 2002, the People’s Bank cut its own benchmark rate. In real terms, Chinese short-term rates remained negative.[fn3](#section-58)

![](assets/00015-ee1f9207.gif)

[12.](#section-9) The huge gap between deposit rates and nominal GDP growth is a measure of the extent to which Chinese savers were repressed.

On the eve of the global financial crisis, China’s current account surplus reached 10 per cent of GDP. More than half of the country’s national income was being saved. As savings grabbed a larger slice of the economic pie, household consumption as a share of GDP fell to little more than half the US level. The removal of the ‘iron rice bowl’ (the universal welfare policy of the Mao era) is often held responsible for China’s savings glut and massive trade surpluses. Yet the data show only a slight increase in household savings (as a proportion of GDP) after 1990, and most of those savings came from the wealthy elite.[21](#section-53) During this period workers’ incomes actually lagged behind economic growth, and household savings fell as a proportion of total savings.[22](#section-53)

Financial repression was largely responsible for this state of affairs.[fn4](#section-58) In *The Great Rebalancing* (2013), Peking University professor Michael Pettis calculated the costs to household savers and benefits to borrowers from artificially depressed deposit rates. ‘The total transfer from households to state-owned enterprises, infrastructure investors, and other favored institutions amounts to anywhere from 3 percent to 8 percent of GDP annually,’ Pettis concluded.[23](#section-53) Cheap credit enabled Chinese companies to invest more:[24](#section-53) ‘the problem is not that the household propensity to save is too high,’ wrote Ronald McKinnon, ‘but rather that enterprises save too much – mostly in the form of excess investment in fixed assets.’[25](#section-53) Government savings also climbed thanks to rising receipts on land sales and massive infrastructure investment.[26](#section-53)

Claudio Borio provides an alternative view to the conventional wisdom on Chinese savings. Most people look upon savings as a ‘real’ phenomenon; that’s to say, they assume that savings arise when individuals voluntarily refrain from consuming their income. But this isn’t how things work in the real world, says Borio. In the real world, banks create credit out of thin air. Savings and investment are two sides of the same coin. Thus, when a bank loan is used for the purposes of investment there occurs an automatic increase in reported savings.[27](#section-53) In China, financial repression stimulated credit growth; much of the new credit was invested, which, in turn, pushed up the savings rate.

### UNSTABLE, UNBALANCED, UNCOORDINATED AND UNSUSTAINABLE

In March 2007, Premier Wen Jiabao observed that China’s economy was ‘unstable, unbalanced, uncoordinated, and unsustainable’. Presumably Wen had in mind the depressed level of household consumption and sky-high investment rate, funded by vast domestic savings. The failure of economic co-ordination identified by Premier Wen is what Hayek suggested would happen when interest rates are kept below their natural level. But Premier Wen’s comment, repeated on subsequent occasions, bore his ‘signature combination of noble sentiment and missing action’.[28](#section-53) No significant reforms were embarked upon. Since the authorities wouldn’t countenance a downturn, imbalances were allowed to fester. As a senior Beijing official reportedly said, ‘A little bit more imbalance … is better than a lot of collapse.’[29](#section-53)

Beijing responded to the global financial crisis by launching a massive economic stimulus in November 2008. The stimulus carried a headline figure of 4 trillion yuan (12.5 per cent of GDP), with most of the money supplied by banks. Over the course of 2009, credit expanded by more than 30 per cent of GDP. Financial repression became more deeply entrenched. In the month after Lehman’s bankruptcy the People’s Bank cut interest rates twice.[30](#section-53) By January 2009, China’s interbank rate stood at 1 per cent, down 4 percentage points since the previous summer.[31](#section-53) Over the following five years, the benchmark rate averaged less than 1 per cent in real terms and trailed far below the country’s nominal GDP growth. The yuan continued to be loosely pegged to the US dollar. Foreign capital continued to pour into the country. The People’s Bank continued printing money to buy dollars.[fn5](#section-58)

Although China’s current account surplus declined after the global financial crisis, its foreign exchange reserves doubled between 2008 and 2014, reaching a total of more than $4 trillion. By the latter date, up to a third of these reserves derived from foreign capital inflows.[32](#section-53) Not all of these inflows came from Western investors. Chinese multinationals borrowed in dollars through their foreign subsidiaries and exchanged the dollars for yuan, which they used for investment or lent onwards at higher rates outside the formal banking system.[33](#section-53) Foreign bank claims on China reached $1.7 trillion in 2014.[34](#section-53)

Thanks to the near limitless supply of cheap credit, China’s imbalances grew larger. As Bloomberg’s Tom Orlik writes,

> State-owned industrial giants went deep into debt, paying for new steel mills, coal mines, and cement kilns, adding to already burgeoning overcapacity. Real estate developers painted their balance sheets in red ink, borrowing to build ghost towns of unsold property. Local governments dodged the regulations intended to keep public debt under control, creating opaque investment vehicles to borrow off the books.[35](#section-53)

China’s financial repression came in the form of *unstable* bubbles, *uncoordinated* investment, *unsustainable* debt, and an *unbalanced* shadow banking system, and it also allowed *unscrupulous* vested interests, including members of Premier Wen’s own family, to reap the benefits from the limitless flow of easy money.

### UNSTABLE BUBBLES

‘There’s always a bubble in China,’ a world-weary fund manager told the *Wall Street Journal* in November 2016. There was no disputing this. Over the previous years a bewildering array of mini-bubbles had popped up across the country, ranging from a caterpillar fungus with aphrodisiac properties to garlic bulbs; from vintage claret to China’s home-grown bubbly, Moutai; from works of fine art to fine china; and bubbles in just about every industrial commodity, from copper to iron ore. The Shanghai stock market witnessed a succession of magnificent bubbles. Overshadowing them all was an epic real estate bubble that proved resilient in adversity, shaped the country’s economic development and was the ultimate source of all those other bubbles.

By October 2007 the Shanghai stock market was up more than fourfold in a little over eighteen months. The combined value of listed companies was more than twice China’s GDP. Monetary policy contributed to the stock market boom. At the time, the central bank was printing and selling billions of yuan to maintain the dollar peg. In July 2005, the central bank had allowed the yuan to appreciate but offset this move by lowering interest rates (which remained negative in real terms). Bank credit was allowed to expand dramatically.[36](#section-53) Nearly two decades earlier, the Bank of Japan had followed a similar path, loosening monetary conditions in the wake of the international currency agreement known as the Plaza Accord. Japan expert Peter Tasker drew a parallel between these two episodes:

> As with Japan in the 1980s, China’s monetary policy has become a hostage to its export machine. Interest rates are held far below their natural level in order to restrain the yuan. At the same time, financial liberalization has opened the securities markets to millions of unsophisticated Chinese investors who finally have an alternative to value-losing bank deposits. It is hard to imagine a more bubble-worthy set of circumstances.[37](#section-53)

In the months following the October 2007 peak, the Shanghai stock market declined by more than 70 per cent. Beijing’s stimulus soon came to the rescue of beleaguered speculators, however. By the summer of 2009, the Shanghai Composite had nearly doubled from its trough. The dollar value of shares traded in Shanghai exceeded the combined turnover of the stock exchanges in London, New York and Tokyo. Seven Chinese companies made the list of the world’s ten largest companies by market value.

The stock market frenzy abated towards the end of 2009, but not for long. Between November 2014 and the summer of 2015, the Shanghai Composite doubled once again. Once again, animal spirits were stoked by Beijing, this time to offset weakness in the housing market. The central bank lowered its benchmark rate and expanded its own balance sheet.
