After restrictions on brokers’ loans were relaxed, margin loans grew to exceed $1 trillion.[38](#section-53) Technology shares sold for more than two hundred times earnings, ‘making the heady days of the dot-com bubble look tame by comparison’.[39](#section-53) The IPO of China National Nuclear Power in early June was oversubscribed by 137 times, locking up $273 billion in subscriptions. The shares increased by 44 per cent on the first day’s trading.

This speculative fever was also short-lived. By July 2015, the Shanghai Composite was down by a third. Trading halts were declared for a majority of stocks. Fearful of a complete market rout, Beijing strove to create an environment of ‘positive energy’. Regulators and censors warned citizens against making negative comments about the economy. The central bank cut interest rates and bank reserve requirements, and lent money to prop up the market. A ‘national team’ of state enterprises borrowed large sums to buy shares.[fn6](#section-58) At the graduation ceremony at Tsinghua University, students were instructed to ‘shout loudly the slogan, “revive the A shares, benefit the people; revive the A shares, benefit the people.”’[40](#section-53)

The ups and downs of the stock market were a sideshow compared to developments in China’s property market. During the global financial crisis, house prices dipped sharply in Beijing and other leading cities. The authorities acted forcefully to turn the tide. Banks were ordered to ease lending standards and provide more second mortgages. Housebuyers were able to borrow at a large discount to the benchmark rate. Over the course of 2009, mortgage lending quintupled and property sales rose by two-thirds.[41](#section-53) The *Wall Street Journal* reported on a rush to buy land in Beijing. House prices in Tier 1 cities – the world’s hottest real estate, according to Savills – climbed by more than two-thirds.

China overtook the United States to become the world’s largest property market by value.[42](#section-53) At which point, the authorities decided to cool the housing market. Interest rates and bank capital requirements were hiked in early 2010 and mortgage standards tightened. Banks were instructed to stop lending for third-home purchases.[43](#section-53) It took a while for these measures to bite, but towards the end of 2011 property prices were falling in nearly all of the seventy cities tracked by the National Bureau of Statistics. House sales crashed in Shanghai and Beijing. Whereupon policy was reversed again. In the summer of 2012, interest rates were cut as part of a ‘global coordinated global easing campaign’ (according to Bloomberg) linked to Europe’s sovereign debt crisis.

Having survived numerous setbacks, China’s property market gained a reputation for invincibility – a key condition, according to hedge fund tycoon George Soros, for a ‘super bubble’ to emerge. After the 2015 stock market crash, monetary policy was further eased. In October, the central bank’s benchmark rate reached an all-time low of 2 per cent. Over the following year, bank lending accelerated, with mortgages taking a greater share of new loans.[44](#section-53) In parts of Shanghai and neighbouring Suzhou, empty development plots sold for more than neighbouring land with completed buildings – a case of ‘flour more expensive than bread’. By late 2016, house prices were valued nationwide at eight times average Chinese incomes, roughly double the peak valuation of US housing a decade earlier.

Property valuations in China weren’t completely irrational. Sir James Steuart’s claim that the value of the Mississippi Company was justified by the low cost of borrowing applied to China’s real estate market. John Law’s Royal Bank set interest rates at 2 per cent in 1719. Nearly three centuries later, the People’s Bank set interest rates at the same level. A study released in 2015 by the National Bureau of Economic Research found that rental yields in Beijing and Shanghai had fallen below 2 per cent – in line with the discount rate.[45](#section-53) However, rental yields of less than 2 per cent implied a payback of nearly seven decades – roughly the same length of time as residential land leases, after which title reverted to the state. China’s property market was hailed as the ‘bubble that never pops’.[46](#section-53) But, as the NBER researchers commented, ‘only modest declines in expected appreciation seem needed to generate large drops in house values.’

By late 2016 total real estate was valued at $43 trillion, equivalent to nearly four times GDP and on a par with the aggregate value of Japanese real estate (relative to GDP) at its bubble peak.[47](#section-53) Like Japan three decades earlier, China had transformed into a ‘land bubble’ economy. The French bank Société Générale had calculated back in 2011 that over the previous decade China had built 16 billion square metres of residential floor space. This was equivalent to building modern Rome from scratch every fourteen days, over and over again. A decade after the stimulus more than half of the world’s hundred tallest buildings were under construction in the People’s Republic, and more than a quarter of economic output was related, directly or indirectly, to real estate development.[48](#section-53)

The ostensible rationale for China’s incredible building spree was urban migration. Yet while hordes of migrants worked on construction sites, they couldn’t afford to acquire the properties they built. Instead, much of the demand for new homes came from investors. In November 2009, Melissa Chan of Al Jazeera TV reported on the new development of Ordos (also known as Kangbashi) in Inner Mongolia.[49](#section-53) Built in five years, the city was intended to house over a million people. However, when Chan visited Ordos she found nothing but ‘empty homes, new and neat, block after block’. The apartments had reportedly been snapped up by rich Mongolian miners as investments. Overnight, Ordos became the world’s most famous ‘ghost city’.

Many new apartments in China were sold as concrete shells, known as ‘blank houses’ (*maopeifang*), that lacked basic amenities such as electric wiring and plumbing. Many remained in this unoccupied state for years on end. Absentee apartment owners saved money by not servicing elevators, which led to the occasional tragic accident.[fn7](#section-58) Vacant residential blocks could be identified at night by their darkened windows. In 2010, it was widely reported that some 65 million properties connected to the power grid were not using any electricity.[50](#section-53) Later estimates suggested that a fifth of the urban housing stock remained unoccupied.[51](#section-53) China was said to have enough empty properties to house the entire population of Canada.[52](#section-53)

China’s real estate bubble threatened the country’s economic miracle, by lowering productivity growth and fuelling corruption.[53](#section-53) As a retired senior Beijing official described the situation: ‘The real estate industry’s excessive prosperity has not only kidnapped local governments but also kidnapped financial institutions – restraining and even harming the development of the real economy, inflating asset bubbles and accumulating debt risk.’[54](#section-53) Real estate was the one thing in China more powerful than its imperial President. In December 2016, Xi Jinping proclaimed that ‘houses are for living in, not for speculation.’ Yet at the time nearly a third of Chinese families owned one or more vacant properties.[55](#section-53) Such was the nation’s devotion to property that the divorce rate spiked after Beijing imposed restrictions on families owning more than a single property.[56](#section-53)

### UNCOORDINATED INVESTMENT

Beijing’s stimulus plan launched thousands of ‘shovel-ready’ projects for new airports, bridges, highways, subways, and so forth. The most ambitious scheme involved the rapid expansion of the high-speed rail network, reportedly the world’s most expensive public works project since the US interstate highways were built in the 1950s.[57](#section-53) The person in charge of this mega-project was Railway Minister Liu Zhijun, whose Maoist exhortation that ‘To achieve a great leap, an entire generation must be sacrificed’ earned him the sobriquet ‘Great Leap Liu’. Spending on the project amounted to 2 per cent of China’s GDP.

By 2010, the Railway Ministry owed more than 1 trillion yuan on railway bonds alone. Alongside the inevitable cost overruns, there were rumours that cheap materials had been used by contractors, a practice known as ‘robbing the beams to put in the pillar’. Safety fears came to a head on 23 July 2011, when a bullet train bound for Fuzhou collided with another train outside Wenzhou, killing forty passengers and injuring many more. By this date, Liu was under investigation for ‘severe violations of discipline’. The Minister had received kickbacks on construction contracts, operated a slush fund to bribe newspaper editors and maintained no fewer than eighteen mistresses. (In July 2013 a court sentenced the former rail chief to death, commuted to life imprisonment.)

The legacy of the high-speed rail expansion was a massive waste of resources, mountains of debt, an economy addicted to construction spending, and public corruption on an epic scale. Writ large, this is the story of China’s recent economic development. When the cost of borrowing is low enough, even the most absurd investments can appear viable. In twenty-first-century China, easy money levelled mountains. Or, more precisely, the local government in the city of Shiyan, Hubei province, ordered that local mountains be flattened to make space for new manufacturing plants. ‘Levelling mountains,’ declared the local land bureau, ‘has become the golden key to resolve the problem of Shiyan’s development impasse.’[58](#section-53)

Spending on infrastructure normally tracks economic development: bridges are built, tunnels dug and railway tracks laid because there is an existing demand for their services. In China, however, investment plans were lifted from the *Field of Dreams*’ script: ‘if you build it, he will come.’ New infrastructure would supposedly drive urbanization and boost productivity. But researchers at Oxford’s business school found that ‘Far from being an engine of economic growth, a typical infrastructure investment has destroyed economic value in China.’[59](#section-53)

Among the other high-profile infrastructure projects at this time were a new airport south of Beijing said to be the size of Bermuda, and the world’s longest bridge, linking Hong Kong to the Mainland. China’s mandarins have a long tradition of authorizing impressive investments. The Grand Canal, the world’s longest waterway, was built in the seventh century with the forced labour of millions. ‘What is to be wondered at in China,’ wrote the Dominican monk Gaspar da Cruz in the sixteenth century, ‘is that there are bridges in uninhabited places throughout the country, and these are not less well built nor less costly than those which are nigh the cities, but rather they are all costly and very well wrought.’[60](#section-53) In the Immobile Empire some things never change.

Investment wasn’t merely directed towards infrastructure projects. As part of the stimulus, Beijing endorsed a ‘strategic emerging industries’ plan, promoting investment in new technologies, including biotech and electric vehicles.[61](#section-53) A number of sectors, ranging from aerospace to telecoms, were earmarked for ‘indigenous innovation’.[62](#section-53) Several ‘engineering mega-projects’ were fast-tracked, including a plan to develop a large-scale civilian jet-liner. Less glamorous industries were also supported with stimulus funds, including machinery, textiles, shipbuilding, car-making, steel, nonferrous metals and logistics. The trouble was that most of these industries already produced more than they could sell.[63](#section-53)

The glut in China’s steel production was notorious. Before the financial crisis, the People’s Republic produced around half of the world’s steel at a time when its steel companies were operating at just two-thirds of capacity.[64](#section-53) The boom in real estate and infrastructure created a much-needed surge in the demand for steel. But all the extra investment in steel plants meant supply continued to outstrip demand. Steel prices collapsed, falling to the point where it was said that ‘steel was cheaper than cabbage’.[fn8](#section-58)

A number of other industries, including cement, flat glass, paper, solar and wind power, were likewise afflicted by the twin scourges of overinvestment and oversupply.[65](#section-53) As with steel, the stimulus pushed cement demand through the roof. A much-cited factoid from the US Geological Survey claimed that in the three years after 2008 China consumed nearly one and a half times as much cement as the United States had used over the course of the twentieth century. On an annual basis, nearly two tonnes of cement were poured for every man, woman and child in the world’s most populous country.[66](#section-53) Nevertheless, China’s cement industry continued to be plagued with excess capacity and continued to add yet more capacity.

State-owned enterprises received the lion’s share of cheap bank credit, together with numerous other subsidies.[fn9](#section-58) But their access to low-cost capital had a negative impact on returns on capital. By 2014 state-owned enterprises were earning just half as much as their private counterparts.[67](#section-53) As their asset base expanded, their profitability declined.[68](#section-53)

As in Europe, China’s economy became infested with corporate zombies, nourished on a diet of cheap credit, state subsidies and loan forbearance. In January 2016 the *People’s Daily* carried an interview with an ‘authoritative person’, believed to be President Xi’s chief economic adviser, Liu He, who called for a reduction in industrial overcapacity.[69](#section-53) Premier Li Keqiang reinforced this message, declaring that ‘For those “zombie enterprises” with absolute overcapacity, we must ruthlessly bring down the knife.’[70](#section-53) A number of supply-side reforms were announced and two loss-making state-owned steelmakers – Baosteel and Wuhan Steel – were merged.[71](#section-53) Yet only a few months after the Premier’s comments, US steelmakers complained that Chinese competitors were being kept alive with state subsidies and dumping their surplus steel in the United States.[72](#section-53) The IMF identified some 3,500 state-owned zombies across eleven Chinese provinces.[73](#section-53)

What the *People’s Daily* called the ‘development disease’ inflicted an immense social and environmental toll.[74](#section-53) Home to a fifth of the world’s population, the People’s Republic consumed around half of the world’s production of steel, cement, copper, aluminium, nickel and coal.[75](#section-53) In 2009, China overtook the United States to become the world’s leading producer of greenhouse gases. Between 2000 and 2014, China’s annual carbon emissions trebled.[76](#section-53) ‘When an economy as large as China’s,’ writes economic analyst Henry Maxey, ‘can engineer an unproductive infrastructure boom through abuse of a pure credit system, we should not be surprised to see global carbon dioxide emissions rising … monetary policy has catalysed activities that have accelerated the problem.’[77](#section-53)

Capital was misallocated in China on a scale not seen since the heyday of the Soviet Union. Soviet central planners had also operated under conditions of financial repression. In his *Political Economy of Socialism*, Hungarian economist János Kornai explained how monetary conditions in Communist Russia and its satellites contributed to their economic failure:

> [M]arket coordination had not become predominant in these economies. If the real interest rate is negative for a long period, it is unable to control the allocation of investments and gives false information to decision makers for all the decisions that compare present and future revenues and expenditures.[78](#section-53)

In 1994, Paul Krugman published a celebrated essay in *Foreign Affairs* entitled ‘The ‘Myth of Asia’s Miracle’. Krugman observed that ‘Rapid Soviet economic growth [in the 1950s] was based entirely on one attribute: the willingness to save, to sacrifice current consumption for the sake of future production.’[79](#section-53) At a time when the World Bank was hailing an ‘East Asian Economic Miracle’, Krugman pointed out that most Asian economies, like Khrushchev’s Russia, needed ever-increasing investment inputs in order to grow. What Krugman didn’t say was that several Asian economies had pegged their currencies to the US dollar and were funding investment with cheap foreign loans. Not long after this article appeared, the Asian crisis broke.

Krugman’s analysis also applies to China, a country which implemented the ‘Asian development model on steroids’, according to Michael Pettis. As a share of GDP, China invested far more than any other Asian country had ever attempted. As investment climbed to unprecedented levels, the efficiency of investment – what economists call the ‘incremental capital to output ratio’ – spiralled downwards.[fn10](#section-58) All those immense sums spent on bridges, high-speed trains and roads were failing to generate the much-touted improvements to productivity. The People’s Republic was trapped on an investment ‘treadmill to hell’.[80](#section-53) But stepping off the treadmill would amount to ‘drinking poison to cure thirst’.

### UNSUSTAINABLE DEBT

The surge of credit unleashed by Beijing’s stimulus in 2009 acted like a gigantic defibrillator placed over the heart of a faltering economy. But credit is an addictive substance whose effect diminishes with excessive use. Even as China’s growth slowed over the following years, its economy required ever larger doses. After the stimulus, the boost to GDP from 100 yuan of new credit fell to 30 yuan, around a third of its prior level.[81](#section-53) The waning contribution of credit to economic growth matched the declining efficiency of investment. This was only to be expected since most investment was financed with debt.[82](#section-53)

A nation’s capacity to bear debt is related to its economic development. Rich countries are generally able to shoulder more debt than poorer ones. What made China’s growing indebtedness egregious was that its economy remained relatively undeveloped, with average incomes still far below Western levels. The rapidity of credit growth (relative to GDP) also exceeded most earlier credit booms, including Japan’s in the 1980s, and was roughly on a par with the Spanish and Irish experiences prior to 2008.[83](#section-53) Then, there was the scale. In ten years to 2015, China accounted for around half the world’s total credit creation.[84](#section-53) This borrowing binge constituted ‘history’s greatest Credit Bubble’.[85](#section-53)

Every part of the economy became bloated with debt. Liabilities of the banking system grew to three times GDP. At the time of Lehman’s bankruptcy, households in the People’s Republic carried much less debt than their American counterparts. But, since the much-touted ‘rebalancing’ of the economy never occurred, consumers turned to credit to enhance their purchasing power. Between 2008 and 2018, Chinese households doubled their level of debt (relative to income) and ended up owing more than American households did at the start of the subprime crisis. Over the same period, Chinese companies borrowed $15 trillion, accounting for roughly half the total increase in global corporate debt. Real estate companies borrowed to finance their developments – the largest developer, Evergrande, ran up total liabilities equivalent to 3 per cent of GDP. Local governments set up opaque financing vehicles to pay for infrastructure projects with borrowed money. Debt owed by local governments grew to $8.2 trillion (by the end of 2020), equivalent to more than half of GDP.[86](#section-53)

Although they borrowed more cheaply than private firms, state-owned enterprises nevertheless had trouble covering their interest costs.[fn11](#section-58) After 2012 the total cost of debt-servicing exceeded China’s economic growth.[87](#section-53) An economy that can’t grow faster than its interest costs is said to have entered a ‘debt trap’. China avoided the immediate consequences of the debt trap by concealing bad debts. What’s been called ‘Red Capitalism’ resembled a shell game in which non-performing loans were passed from one state-connected player to another.

The shell game commenced at the turn of this century when state banks were weighed down with non-performing loans. The bad loans weren’t written off, however, but sold at face value to state-owned asset management companies (AMCs), which paid for them by issuing ten-year bonds that were, in turn, acquired by the state-owned banks. In effect, the banks had swapped uncollectible short-term debt for uncollectible long-dated debt. When the day finally arrived for the AMCs to redeem their bonds, the loans were quietly rolled over. Concealing or ‘evergreening’ bad debts required low interest rates. China’s rate cuts in 2001 and 2002 were partly intended to help banks handle their debt problems. Over the following years, bank loan rates were kept well below the country’s nominal GDP growth, while deposit rates remained stuck beneath 3 per cent. Thus, Chinese depositors indirectly bailed out the banking system.[88](#section-53)

After 2008, cracks in the credit system were papered over with new loans – a tenet of Red Capitalism being that ‘as long as the banks continue to lend, there will be no repayment problems.’[89](#section-53) But it became progressively harder to conceal problem loans. In 2015, an industrial engineering company (Baoding Tianwei Group) became the first state-owned enterprise to default on its domestic bonds.[90](#section-53) The trickle of defaults continued. One could only guess at the scale of China’s bad debts. Bank analyst Charlene Chu suggested that by 2017 up to a quarter of bank loans were non-performing. This estimate was five times the official figure.[91](#section-53)

As Chu commented: ‘if losses don’t manifest on financial institution balance sheets, they will do so via slowing growth and deflation.’[92](#section-53) Debt deflation, as Irving Fisher pointed out, occurs after too much debt has accumulated. At the same time, excess industrial capacity was putting downward pressure on producer prices and leading China to export deflation abroad – for instance, by dumping its surplus steel in European and US markets. Corporate zombies added to deflation pressures. Despite the soaring money supply after 2008, consumer prices hardly budged. By November 2015, the index of producer prices had fallen for a record forty-four consecutive months.[93](#section-53)

If China’s investment had been productive, then it would have generated the cash flow needed to pay off its debt. But, for the economy as a whole, this wasn’t the case.[94](#section-53) So debt continued growing. Top officials in Beijing were aware that the situation was unsustainable. In the summer of 2016, President Xi’s anonymous adviser warned in his interview with the *People’s Daily* that leverage must be contained. ‘A tree cannot grow to the sky,’ declared the ‘authoritative person’; ‘high leverage must bring with it high risks.’[95](#section-53) Former Finance Minister Lou Jiwei put his finger on Beijing’s dilemma: ‘The first problem is to stop the accumulation of leverage,’ Lou said. ‘But we also can’t allow the economy to lose speed.’[96](#section-53) Since these twin ambitions are incompatible, Beijing chose the path of least resistance. A decade after the stimulus launch, China’s ‘Great Wall of Debt’ had reached 250 per cent of GDP, up 100 percentage points since 2008.[97](#section-53) There was still more to come.

### UNBALANCED SHADOW BANKING

In 1984, the first private money house in Communist China opened in Wenzhou, a coastal city in the south-eastern province of Zhejiang. Founded by a former hospital administrator named Fang, the Ascendant Money House of Cangnan County provided credit to local businesses. At the time state-run banks monopolized lending, but opened for only a few hours each day and lent only to those with political connections. The banks took months to approve a loan. By contrast, Fang’s business was open 24/7. Business was so brisk that the moneylender charged interest on an hourly basis: ‘Time is interest’ was his motto.[98](#section-53)

A double-track system of interest rates emerged in China after 1979. Cheap loans were originated by state banks for state-owned enterprises, and more costly credit was provided by back-alley banks to private enterprises. A few years after the establishment of Fang’s Money House, dozens of competitors were operating in Wenzhou. Among them were credit associations, credit co-operatives and pawnshops – the latter an ancient Chinese institution dating back to the period of the Six Dynasties early in the first millennium of the Common Era. Wenzhou’s informal lending market was roiled by occasional pyramid schemes and constantly harassed by state banks. Naturally, the People’s Bank of China disapproved. The Ascendant Money House, along with several other money houses and credit co-operatives, was ‘rectified’ – that’s to say, closed down – in the late 1980s.

Public officials complained that Wenzhou’s loan sharks exploited borrowers. In fact, their high interest charges served to ration capital, ensuring that money went to businesses that made the best use of it. To avoid accusations of profiteering, rural co-operatives charged what they called a ‘capital use fee’ – as good a definition of interest as any other – and entered loans into their books as ‘capital managed by another person’. Despite their seamy aspects, back-alley banks financed tens of thousands of local businesses in Wenzhou, many involved in the mass production of watches, spectacles, cigarette lighters and shoes for export. The same story was repeated across the People’s Republic, where countless entrepreneurs established businesses with the help of informal lenders.

In Fang’s day the main business of Wenzhou’s unofficial credit system was supplying entrepreneurs with working capital. After 2008, however, profits from local manufacturing were squeezed by rising commodity costs and slowing exports. So, lenders turned to financing speculation. Wenzhou merchants were said to be the moving force behind a number of bubbles, from garlic bulbs to holiday homes on Hainan Island. By giving up traditional manufacturing for speculation, they ‘cast off the real for the empty’.

Real estate was the prime object of speculation, financed with loans from back-alley lenders.[99](#section-53) In the post-stimulus period, Wenzhou property prices doubled. Prime locations became nearly as costly as those of Shanghai and Beijing.[100](#section-53) Apartments in the grandly named ‘Versailles Residential de Luxe La Grande Maison’ were marketed at $11,000 a square metre – more expensive than Mayfair or Manhattan.[101](#section-53) Wenzhou gave off every appearance of prosperity. Its streets were lined with car dealerships for luxury marques – an online video of a Wenzhou wedding motorcade, featuring a procession of Rolls-Royces, Bentleys, Ferraris and Lamborghinis, went viral.[102](#section-53)

Towards the middle of 2011, however, the city’s informal banking system suddenly imploded. The proximate cause of the credit crunch was recent interest-rate hikes by the People’s Bank.[fn12](#section-58) The panic started after a local industrial park defaulted on its loans.[103](#section-53) A few months earlier, the owner of the country’s largest spectacle manufacturer had disappeared, leaving behind large debts to private lenders. Pawnshops, credit companies and loan sharks called in their loans and raised their lending rates. More businessmen upped sticks. Wenzhou merchants rushed to dump properties acquired with underground loans. As property prices sagged, more creditors called in their loans. A property sales manager recalled a ‘stampede, like animals running for their lives from a wild bushfire’.[104](#section-53) The city’s network of credit guarantee businesses fell like dominoes. Outside closed factory gates, police fought demonstrations by unpaid workers.

Wenzhou’s credit crunch attracted widespread attention at home and abroad. Premier Wen visited the city, accompanied by the Finance Minister and the head of the central bank. His mission was to ‘stop the horse at the edge of the cliff’. Banks were ordered to lend and credit conditions were relaxed – local farmers were even allowed to post pigs as collateral for loans.[105](#section-53) Monetary conditions were eased nationwide. The credit crunch was successfully confined to Zhejiang province.

By this date, back-alley banking of the Wenzhou variety had already been overtaken by a new type of lending, one that also took place outside the formal banking system. As Ronald McKinnon pointed out, financial repression creates an incentive for savers to remove their savings from banks and seek higher returns elsewhere. That’s what happened in the United States at the turn of the century after the Greenspan Fed lowered the Fed funds rate to 1 per cent and sales of structured finance products took off. America’s ‘shadow banks’ spectacularly collapsed in the subprime crisis. After Lehman’s bankruptcy, shadow banking didn’t disappear; instead, it found a new home in the People’s Republic.

The Chinese version of shadow banking comprised a variety of financial products. Most popular was the wealth management product (WMP), a credit instrument sold by banks that generally paid about 2 per cent more than bank deposits and was widely (if falsely) believed to be guaranteed by the issuer. Trust products were riskier, as they were often tied to real estate developments, but paid more. Companies short of cash sold debt-receivables. State-owned enterprises borrowed cheaply from the state banks to provide entrusted loans to private businesses. Online lending was dominated by internet giants Alibaba and Tencent.

By 2016, the market for wealth management products had grown to 23.5 trillion yuan, equivalent to over a third of China’s national income. Total shadow finance was estimated to be twice as large.[106](#section-53) Even the relatively obscure market for debt-receivables exceeded the size of the US subprime market at its peak.[107](#section-53) George Soros observed an ‘eery resemblance’ between China’s shadow banks and the discredited American version.[108](#section-53) Both were driven by a search for yield at a time of low interest rates; both were opaque; both involved banks originating and selling on questionable loans; both depended on the credit markets remaining open and liquid; and both were exposed to real estate bubbles.[109](#section-53)

The People’s Bank had previously controlled interest rates through its authority over bank deposit and lending rates. But as the shadow finance world grew, this tool became ineffective. Banks that were heavily exposed to wealth management products required larger and larger sums to roll over on maturity, with short-term loans provided by other banks. In late June 2013, China’s interbank market suddenly seized up: overnight rates soared to nearly 30 per cent, the Shanghai stock market fell more than 5 per cent and ATMs in Beijing reportedly stopped providing cash. The People’s Bank initially refused to accommodate the banks, to teach them a lesson, but it soon relented. The central bank now turned to managing the volatility of interbank market rates.[110](#section-53) The overnight bank lending rate (known as SHIBOR) was becalmed at 2 per cent.

Shadow finance was quickly integrated into Red Capitalism’s shell game. Not long after the Wenzhou crisis, a wealth management product issued by Huaxia, a small commercial bank, threatened to default. A credit guarantee company with no apparent connection to the stricken credit instrument was brought in to protect investors.[111](#section-53) The following year, a state-run asset management company absorbed a couple of property trusts that were on the verge of collapse.[112](#section-53) In 2015, a coalmining company from Shanxi province defaulted on a $500 million WMP, fatefully named ‘Credit Equals Gold No. 1’. Sure enough, a third party turned up to take over the company’s debts and forgive outstanding interest.[113](#section-53) By putting a safety net under the credit system, Beijing bought stability in the near-term. But stability came at a high cost. It was widely assumed that large borrowers would always be bailed out and certain classes of creditor (including the holders of wealth management products) would always be protected. As a result, interest rates in China didn’t reflect credit risk.[114](#section-53)

Hyman Minsky coined the term ‘Ponzi finance’ to describe the situation when a borrower can’t service its debts from current income and remains solvent only if asset prices continue to rise. As the tenth anniversary of the stimulus approached, the departing Governor of the People’s Bank, Zhou Xiaochuan, warned of ‘hidden, complex, sudden, contagious and hazardous’ risks in China’s credit system.[115](#section-53) The Governor pointed to Ponzi lending schemes operated by internet companies.[fn13](#section-58) (A few months earlier, the collapse of a peer-to-peer lending scheme had prompted large public protests in Beijing’s financial district.[116](#section-53)) He also warned of financial risks from zombie companies, poor risk models, speculative bubbles and financial innovation. The country’s top banker feared that China faced its own ‘Minsky moment’.[117](#section-53)

Not long after, the government seized control of Baoshang Bank, a regional lender based in Baotou, Inner Mongolia. Baoshang had grown rapidly by issuing negotiable certificates of deposit to other banks. Its controlling shareholder had reportedly misused these funds. Zhou’s People’s Bank turned out to have been an unwitting accomplice. Baoshang’s borrowing had taken off after 2013 when the central bank started managing volatility in the interbank loan market.[118](#section-53) Minsky would not have been surprised: in the world of finance capitalism, he said, ‘stability is destabilizing’.

### CAPITAL FLIGHT

The chief reason the authorities could prevent credit problems from escalating was that capital controls trapped domestic savings in China. The logic of financial repression, however, drove savings out of the country in search of better returns abroad. As long as the US Federal Reserve kept interest rates close to zero and continued printing money, the pressure on China’s capital account was limited. But once the Fed moved to tighten monetary policy, as it did five years after the Lehman crisis, large sums of money started to leak out of the People’s Republic.

There were countless ways, legal and illegal, for citizens to evade capital controls. In Macau, casinos provided a ‘laundry service’ taking in yuan and paying out in Hong Kong dollars. Money smugglers got Chinese firms to make out fake import invoices.[119](#section-53) Tourism provided another conduit for capital flight with wealthy Chinese employing friends to take money out of the country – a practice known as ‘Smurfing’. In 2015, the authorities launched a crackdown on capital outflows. Police arrested hundreds of money smugglers.[120](#section-53) Banks were told to tighten their foreign exchange dealings too. Multinational companies operating in China had difficulty repatriating profits. Business travellers faced problems getting hold of US dollars for overseas trips.[121](#section-53)

Foreign acquisitions by Chinese firms provided yet another way to remove capital from the country. In October 2014, a Chinese insurance firm, Anbang Insurance, stumped up almost $2 billion for New York’s Waldorf Astoria, a record price for a US hotel that recalled Japan’s hubristic overseas buying spree some three decades earlier. Anbang more closely resembled a shadow bank than a traditional life insurer. Its best-selling product, ‘Anbang Longevity Sure Win Number 1’, paid a generous income while allowing investors to cash it in after a couple of years. Anbang used the money from sales of this product to acquire foreign hotels, retirement homes, insurance companies and other businesses.

Beijing now clamped down on foreign takeovers. Given its prominent role as shadow banker and serial acquirer of foreign companies, Anbang made a perfect scapegoat. The company was ordered to dispose of its foreign investments. Anbang’s chairman, Wu Xiaohui, a well-connected businessman married to a granddaughter of Deng Xiaoping, was arrested for ‘economic crimes’ (and later sentenced to eighteen years in prison). The company’s assets were seized. Neither international borders nor foreign laws impeded Beijing’s attempts to stop capital flight. In January 2017, a Chinese-Canadian tycoon named Xiao Jianhua, who had been accused of money-laundering, was abducted by plainclothes police from his suite in Hong Kong’s Four Seasons Hotel and spirited back to the Mainland where he was thrown in jail.[122](#section-53) ‘Crocodiles’ – the name given to overreaching business types – were becoming an endangered species.

Beijing might defy international law. But for how long could it defy the laws of economics? As John Law had discovered in 1720, it is not possible for a country to fix the price of its currency on the foreign exchanges while rapidly expanding the domestic money supply. Since 2008 China’s money supply had grown relentlessly relative to the size of its economy and the world’s total money supply. Those trillions of dollars’ worth of foreign exchange reserves provided an illusion of safety since a large chunk was tied up in illiquid investments. Besides, cash deposits in China’s banks far exceeded foreign exchange reserves. If only a fraction of those deposits left the country, however, the People’s Republic would face a debilitating currency crisis.

### UNSCRUPULOUS INTERESTS

Stanford economist Edward Shaw, who together with Ronald McKinnon developed the theory of financial repression, drew attention to its political aspects. Shaw suggested that control over interest rates enhanced the power of civil servants, who got to dispense cheap credit to favoured parties. This fostered cronyism and inequality. Bureaucrats who jealously guarded their monetary powers would resist demands for financial liberalization, he added.[123](#section-53) According to the ‘public choice’ school of economics, rents are created when the state interferes with markets and prices are kept away from equilibrium.[124](#section-53) Financial repression in China created copious rents and fostered crony capitalism.

‘Inordinate swindling is often bound up with a low rate of interest,’ observed that acute financial journalist Karl Marx.[125](#section-53) The Harvard economist John Kenneth Galbraith coined a term, ‘the bezzle’, to describe an economy’s ‘inventory of undisclosed embezzlement’ that varies with the business cycle.[126](#section-53) China’s bezzle was inversely related to the interest rate: as rates went down, the bezzle went up.[fn14](#section-58) Corruption was concentrated in those sectors, such as real estate, mining and construction, that benefited most from easy money. Investment projects were selected according to the size of extractable rents.[127](#section-53) Officials in charge of distributing credit made unauthorized loans and skimmed off interest.[128](#section-53) Networks of corruption were sustained by bribes paid in cash, land, property and shares, and by gifts and lavish entertainments. Officials on VIP junkets at Macau casinos laundered bribes while sating their passion for baccarat.[129](#section-53) The prices achieved from the illicit sale of public offices (i.e., the capitalized value of rents) took off.[130](#section-53) As paper wealth expanded, the Party cadres milked the asset economy and crushed political opposition.[131](#section-53)

As in the West, financial repression tilted the playing field in favour of the rich and well-connected. People with access to cheap credit, and those who controlled real and financial assets, enjoyed windfall gains. Ordinary households deprived of a fair return on savings and small businesses forced to borrow at high rates financed this great wealth transfer. From the early 1980s onwards, the rising incomes of hundreds of millions of Chinese workers contributed to a decline in global inequality. But during this period, China itself transformed from one of the world’s most egalitarian nations into one of the least equal. After 2008, the Gini coefficient for Chinese incomes climbed to 0.49 – an indicator of extreme inequality and more than twice the level at the start of the reform era.[fn15](#section-58)

The inequality problem was worse than the official data suggested.[132](#section-53) A 2010 report from Credit Suisse claimed that ‘illegal or quasi-legal’ income amounted to nearly a third of China’s GDP.[133](#section-53) Much of this grey income derived from rents extracted by Party members. The case of Bo Xilai, the princeling who became Party chief of Chongqing, is instructive. As the head of this sprawling municipality, Bo made a great display of rooting out corruption. But after he fell from grace in 2012 it was revealed that his family was worth hundreds of millions of dollars. Premier Wen’s family fortune was estimated at $2.7 billion.[134](#section-53)

The richest 1 per cent of the population controlled a third of the country’s wealth, while the poorest quartile owned just 1 per cent.[135](#section-53) The real estate bubble was responsible for much of this rise in inequality. Researchers at Peking University found that 70 per cent of household wealth was held in real estate. A quarter of China’s dollar billionaires were real estate moguls.[136](#section-53) At the top of the rich list was Xu Jiayin, boss of property developer China Evergrande, whose fortune (in 2018) was estimated at $40 billion. Many successful property developers turned out to be the offspring of top Party members.[137](#section-53) Local government officials who drove villagers off their land to hand it over to developers acted as ‘engines of inequality’.[138](#section-53)

Financial repression turned back the clock on China’s economic liberalization. Throughout its history, the Middle Kingdom’s progress ‘has an intermittent character and is full of leaps and bounds, regressions and relapses’.[139](#section-53) In general, when the state has been relatively weak and money plentiful, the Middle Kingdom has advanced. Incomes were probably higher in the twelfth century under the relatively laissez-faire Song than in the mid-twentieth century when the Communists came to power. But when the state has shown a more authoritarian character, economic output has stagnated or declined. The mandarins’ desire for total monetary control contributed to Imperial China’s ‘great divergence’ from Western economic development.

In recent years, China has experienced an authoritarian relapse. Paramount leader Xi Jinping exercises imperial powers. An Orwellian system of electronic surveillance tracks the citizenry. Millions of Uighurs are reported to have been locked up in camps. Private companies are required to place the interests of the state before their own. The ‘China 2025’ economic development plans aim to establish Chinese predominance in a number of new technologies, from artificial intelligence to robotics. A system of social credits, which rewards and punishes citizens’ behaviour, will supplement conventional credit. A digital yuan, issued by the People’s Bank, will supplement – or even replace – conventional money. These developments are best summed up by a phrase that became commonplace in the 2010s: ‘the state advances, while the private [sector] retreats.’[140](#section-53)

Financial repression has played a role in this regressive movement. The credit binge launched by the 2008/9 stimulus enhanced Beijing’s sway over the economy. As the state has advanced, productivity growth has declined. Because interest rates neither reflect the return on capital nor credit risk, China’s economy has suffered from the twin evils of capital misallocation and excessive debt. Real estate development, fuelled by low-cost credit, delivered what President Xi called ‘fictional growth’. By 2019 Chinese GDP growth (per capita) had fallen to half its 2007 level.

The Third Plenum of the Eighteenth Chinese Communist Party Congress, held in Beijing in 2013, heralded profound reforms to banking practices. The ceiling on bank deposit rates was lifted, and banks could set their own lending rates. Households earned a little more on their bank deposits, but interest rates remained below nominal GDP growth. The central bank now turned to managing the volatility of the interbank market interest rate.[141](#section-53) The People’s Bank still lacked independence and had to appeal to the State Council for any change to monetary policy.

Allowing interest rates to be set by the market would have required wrenching changes. Forced to compete for deposits, state-controlled banks would suffer a loss of profitability. Bad loans would become harder to conceal. Without access to subsidized credit, state-owned enterprises would become even less profitable. Corporate zombies would keel over. Economic planners would lose the ability to direct cheap capital to favoured sectors. The cost of controlling the currency on the foreign exchanges would become prohibitively expensive. Beijing would no longer be able to manipulate real estate or fine-tune other markets.[142](#section-53)

The Party’s monopoly of power has survived the liberalization of most commercial prices and many business activities, but the cadres never removed their grip on the most important price of all. The state, not the market, would determine the level of interest. The legacy of China’s financial repression was, as President Xi told the National Congress in 2017, a ‘contradiction between unbalanced and inadequate [economic] development and the people’s ever-growing needs for a better life’, which, in turn, provided Xi with a rationale for further advancing the role of the state.[143](#section-53)

<!-- rl-section id="sec-chapter018" class="titlepage" title="18" -->

## Financial Repression with Chinese Characteristics

> *[T]he biggest problem with China’s economy is that the growth is unstable, unbalanced, uncoordinated and unsustainable.*
>
> Premier Wen Jiabao, 2007

Successful economic development requires that credit be allocated efficiently. That job is ill done when the state retains control over the banking system and when interest rates are set at inappropriate levels. In the early 1970s, Stanford economist Ronald McKinnon coined the pejorative term ‘financial repression’ to describe the negative consequences of keeping interest rates below the level of inflation. Under such circumstances, borrowers benefit at the expense of savers. Market forces no longer determine how credit is dispensed. Banks become risk averse, preferring to lend to large corporations and state-related entities. Savers look to protect their wealth from inflation by investing in real estate or taking their money abroad. In short, financial repression stifles economic development and weakens the financial system.[1](#section-53)

Financial repression might be said to have been invented in China. The tradition of controlling interest rates dates back as far as the Han period at the beginning of the Common Era.[2](#section-53) The Tang capped interest charged by private lenders while lending their own money at higher rates through the offices of ‘money-catching clerks’.[3](#section-53) Under the Song, guilds were forced to lend to the government at below market rates. The Mongols lent at very favourable rates to Uighur merchants, who ‘used the funds in money lending and various other business enterprises, including foreign trade’. China’s first state bonds were issued only in the late nineteenth century and even then some officials questioned whether the Emperor should have to pay interest.[fn1](#section-58)

Given the insecurity of commerce and the immaturity of financial development in the Middle Kingdom, ‘land purchase was the only method of investment.’[4](#section-53) Loans secured by property attracted the lowest interest. This attitude is summed up in Chang Ying’s *Remarks on a Regular Livelihood*, written in the early Qing period:

> I have seen much of this world. Pawnbroking, trade, and lending at compound interest are such that one inevitably comes to ruin before long. Even if at first you quickly make rich profits, it is certain to come to nothing in the end. Only land and houses can be for long relied upon.[5](#section-53)

Although paper money was invented in China, the verdict of most historians on the country’s monetary history is damning: ‘from having begun as a brilliant solution to a shortage of copper cash, paper money gradually turned into a bureaucratic monstrosity that hampered the productive forces whose growth it had originally done much to foster.’[6](#section-53) Financial repression served as a tool of political repression.[fn2](#section-58) In his brilliant account of Lord Marcartney’s embassy to the Court of Qianlong, Alain Peyrefitte comments that ‘the exploitation of poverty by usurers was all China knew of capitalism. Even this, however, was not really capitalism, but its opposite: money was made not to be invested but to be spent.’[7](#section-53)

### THE REFORM ERA

In 1974, when Deng Xiaoping led a delegation of officials to a special session of the United Nations in New York, there was scarcely enough foreign currency in the whole of China to finance the trip: the sum total of foreign currency that could be located in Beijing’s banks was just $38,000.[8](#section-53) At the time, the People’s Bank of China was a branch of the Ministry of Finance. Yet by 2010 the People’s Republic had transformed into a financial superpower. Its central bank sat on the world’s largest pile of foreign exchange reserves. The China Development Bank, one of several policy banks, was the world’s largest bank by assets. Two publicly listed Chinese banks were ranked among the top ten most valuable companies.[9](#section-53) Outstanding bank loans exceeded China’s GDP.[10](#section-53)

The period of rapid economic growth commenced with Deng’s economic reforms, launched in the late 1970s. Financial deepening – defined as the accumulation of financial assets faster than non-financial wealth – played an important role in what has been called the China miracle.[11](#section-53) World Bank economists Robert King and Ross Levine find a strong relationship between the expansion of the financial sector and subsequent income growth. Their research suggests that finance leads growth, rather than the other way around. As King and Levine write, ‘When countries have relatively high levels of financial development, economic growth tends to be relatively fast over the next 10 to 30 years.’[12](#section-53)

China’s blistering economic growth in the decades after 1980 appeared to support this finding. By the time of the global financial crisis, however, its economy was beset by a number of severe imbalances – asset price bubbles and credit booms, excess savings and wasteful investments. These imbalances were the product of financial repression, according to McKinnon. In a 2012 paper written shortly before his death, McKinnon suggested that negative real interest rates on Chinese bank deposits had reduced household income. Benchmark rates kept below the market-clearing rate were creating an excessive demand for credit, he added.

State-owned enterprises, which received preferential access to credit, were crowding out private businesses, McKinnon suggested. Low interest rates had boosted investment, but the general quality of lending was poor. Furthermore, savings were moving out of banks into an opaque shadow banking system.[13](#section-53) Financial repression had tilted China’s economy away from consumption towards low-quality investment and fostered asset price bubbles. If *financial deepening* made the China miracle, *financial repression* threatened to undo it.

### HOW FINANCIAL REPRESSION WORKS

Here’s how financial repression was implemented in China. Capital controls trapped savings within the country. Households had little choice but to deposit their savings at one of the large banks. The ‘Big Four’ banks were majority owned and tightly controlled by the state. The central bank set the deposit rate below China’s rate of economic growth, and often below the rate of inflation. Banks lent to state enterprises at below market rates. Since the deposit rate was fixed even lower, the banks were guaranteed fat profits. Government-controlled corporations used the cheap credit they received for investment, often favouring sectors selected by Beijing’s economic planners. Banks and state enterprises were the main beneficiaries of financial repression; household savers were the big losers.

The state control of money and interest and the distribution of cheap credit to favoured parties belong to a venerable Chinese tradition. In Deng’s reform era, however, Beijing copied directly from its Asian neighbours. The Asian economic development model, which relied on driving up exports and large-scale investment, had helped the region’s backward economies catch up with their Western competitors.[14](#section-53) In the 1960s South Korea’s government under General Park Chung-hee used state banks to provide loans at negative real interest rates to exporters and favoured industrial projects.[15](#section-53) China adopted the South Korean template.

Financial repression became firmly established towards the end of the 1990s. At the start of the decade, the People’s Bank applied high interest rates to squeeze inflation out of the system. The currency was devalued in early 1994 and later pegged at a significantly undervalued level to the US dollar. To prevent the yuan from appreciating too rapidly, which would have hurt Chinese exports, the People’s Bank intervened in the foreign exchange markets to sell yuan and buy dollars. The dollar securities acquired in this manner were added to the country’s foreign exchange reserves. Thus, China found itself lending indirectly to American consumers for them to buy its exports. Its massive purchases of American securities put downward pressure on US long-term interest rates.

Joining the Dollar Bloc suited Beijing’s mercantilist inclinations. In December 2001, China became a member of the World Trade Organization. This move coincided with the inception of Alan Greenspan’s easy money policy. The People’s Bank kept interest rates low to maintain the dollar peg. Financial repression emerged as a ‘consequence of the government’s policy of maintaining an undervalued exchange rate’.[16](#section-53) Exports and export-driven investment became the main contributors to China’s economic miracle. In the six years after joining the WTO, exports compounded at a mindboggling annual rate of 30 per cent. In 2007, China overtook the United States to become the world’s top exporter.[17](#section-53) Foreign capital poured into the country, driven by expectations that the yuan would appreciate. China’s low interest rates were partly intended to discourage these hot money flows.[18](#section-53)

Much of the new money created by the central bank’s foreign exchange interventions ended up as deposits in Chinese banks, further easing monetary conditions.[19](#section-53) Another consequence of the dollar peg was that domestic monetary policy was increasingly influenced by the decisions taken by the Federal Reserve. The People’s Bank was commonly believed to target a 2.5 percentage point spread above the Fed funds rate.[20](#section-53) A month after the Fed lowered its rate to 1.5 per cent in January 2002, the People’s Bank cut its own benchmark rate. In real terms, Chinese short-term rates remained negative.[fn3](#section-58)

![](assets/00015-ee1f9207.gif)

[12.](#section-9) The huge gap between deposit rates and nominal GDP growth is a measure of the extent to which Chinese savers were repressed.

On the eve of the global financial crisis, China’s current account surplus reached 10 per cent of GDP. More than half of the country’s national income was being saved. As savings grabbed a larger slice of the economic pie, household consumption as a share of GDP fell to little more than half the US level. The removal of the ‘iron rice bowl’ (the universal welfare policy of the Mao era) is often held responsible for China’s savings glut and massive trade surpluses. Yet the data show only a slight increase in household savings (as a proportion of GDP) after 1990, and most of those savings came from the wealthy elite.[21](#section-53) During this period workers’ incomes actually lagged behind economic growth, and household savings fell as a proportion of total savings.[22](#section-53)

Financial repression was largely responsible for this state of affairs.[fn4](#section-58) In *The Great Rebalancing* (2013), Peking University professor Michael Pettis calculated the costs to household savers and benefits to borrowers from artificially depressed deposit rates. ‘The total transfer from households to state-owned enterprises, infrastructure investors, and other favored institutions amounts to anywhere from 3 percent to 8 percent of GDP annually,’ Pettis concluded.[23](#section-53) Cheap credit enabled Chinese companies to invest more:[24](#section-53) ‘the problem is not that the household propensity to save is too high,’ wrote Ronald McKinnon, ‘but rather that enterprises save too much – mostly in the form of excess investment in fixed assets.’[25](#section-53) Government savings also climbed thanks to rising receipts on land sales and massive infrastructure investment.[26](#section-53)

Claudio Borio provides an alternative view to the conventional wisdom on Chinese savings. Most people look upon savings as a ‘real’ phenomenon; that’s to say, they assume that savings arise when individuals voluntarily refrain from consuming their income. But this isn’t how things work in the real world, says Borio. In the real world, banks create credit out of thin air. Savings and investment are two sides of the same coin. Thus, when a bank loan is used for the purposes of investment there occurs an automatic increase in reported savings.[27](#section-53) In China, financial repression stimulated credit growth; much of the new credit was invested, which, in turn, pushed up the savings rate.

### UNSTABLE, UNBALANCED, UNCOORDINATED AND UNSUSTAINABLE

In March 2007, Premier Wen Jiabao observed that China’s economy was ‘unstable, unbalanced, uncoordinated, and unsustainable’. Presumably Wen had in mind the depressed level of household consumption and sky-high investment rate, funded by vast domestic savings. The failure of economic co-ordination identified by Premier Wen is what Hayek suggested would happen when interest rates are kept below their natural level. But Premier Wen’s comment, repeated on subsequent occasions, bore his ‘signature combination of noble sentiment and missing action’.[28](#section-53) No significant reforms were embarked upon. Since the authorities wouldn’t countenance a downturn, imbalances were allowed to fester. As a senior Beijing official reportedly said, ‘A little bit more imbalance … is better than a lot of collapse.’[29](#section-53)

Beijing responded to the global financial crisis by launching a massive economic stimulus in November 2008. The stimulus carried a headline figure of 4 trillion yuan (12.5 per cent of GDP), with most of the money supplied by banks. Over the course of 2009, credit expanded by more than 30 per cent of GDP. Financial repression became more deeply entrenched. In the month after Lehman’s bankruptcy the People’s Bank cut interest rates twice.[30](#section-53) By January 2009, China’s interbank rate stood at 1 per cent, down 4 percentage points since the previous summer.[31](#section-53) Over the following five years, the benchmark rate averaged less than 1 per cent in real terms and trailed far below the country’s nominal GDP growth. The yuan continued to be loosely pegged to the US dollar. Foreign capital continued to pour into the country. The People’s Bank continued printing money to buy dollars.[fn5](#section-58)

Although China’s current account surplus declined after the global financial crisis, its foreign exchange reserves doubled between 2008 and 2014, reaching a total of more than $4 trillion. By the latter date, up to a third of these reserves derived from foreign capital inflows.[32](#section-53) Not all of these inflows came from Western investors. Chinese multinationals borrowed in dollars through their foreign subsidiaries and exchanged the dollars for yuan, which they used for investment or lent onwards at higher rates outside the formal banking system.[33](#section-53) Foreign bank claims on China reached $1.7 trillion in 2014.[34](#section-53)

Thanks to the near limitless supply of cheap credit, China’s imbalances grew larger. As Bloomberg’s Tom Orlik writes,

> State-owned industrial giants went deep into debt, paying for new steel mills, coal mines, and cement kilns, adding to already burgeoning overcapacity. Real estate developers painted their balance sheets in red ink, borrowing to build ghost towns of unsold property. Local governments dodged the regulations intended to keep public debt under control, creating opaque investment vehicles to borrow off the books.[35](#section-53)

China’s financial repression came in the form of *unstable* bubbles, *uncoordinated* investment, *unsustainable* debt, and an *unbalanced* shadow banking system, and it also allowed *unscrupulous* vested interests, including members of Premier Wen’s own family, to reap the benefits from the limitless flow of easy money.

### UNSTABLE BUBBLES

‘There’s always a bubble in China,’ a world-weary fund manager told the *Wall Street Journal* in November 2016. There was no disputing this. Over the previous years a bewildering array of mini-bubbles had popped up across the country, ranging from a caterpillar fungus with aphrodisiac properties to garlic bulbs; from vintage claret to China’s home-grown bubbly, Moutai; from works of fine art to fine china; and bubbles in just about every industrial commodity, from copper to iron ore. The Shanghai stock market witnessed a succession of magnificent bubbles. Overshadowing them all was an epic real estate bubble that proved resilient in adversity, shaped the country’s economic development and was the ultimate source of all those other bubbles.

By October 2007 the Shanghai stock market was up more than fourfold in a little over eighteen months. The combined value of listed companies was more than twice China’s GDP. Monetary policy contributed to the stock market boom. At the time, the central bank was printing and selling billions of yuan to maintain the dollar peg. In July 2005, the central bank had allowed the yuan to appreciate but offset this move by lowering interest rates (which remained negative in real terms). Bank credit was allowed to expand dramatically.[36](#section-53) Nearly two decades earlier, the Bank of Japan had followed a similar path, loosening monetary conditions in the wake of the international currency agreement known as the Plaza Accord. Japan expert Peter Tasker drew a parallel between these two episodes:

> As with Japan in the 1980s, China’s monetary policy has become a hostage to its export machine. Interest rates are held far below their natural level in order to restrain the yuan. At the same time, financial liberalization has opened the securities markets to millions of unsophisticated Chinese investors who finally have an alternative to value-losing bank deposits. It is hard to imagine a more bubble-worthy set of circumstances.[37](#section-53)

In the months following the October 2007 peak, the Shanghai stock market declined by more than 70 per cent. Beijing’s stimulus soon came to the rescue of beleaguered speculators, however. By the summer of 2009, the Shanghai Composite had nearly doubled from its trough. The dollar value of shares traded in Shanghai exceeded the combined turnover of the stock exchanges in London, New York and Tokyo. Seven Chinese companies made the list of the world’s ten largest companies by market value.

The stock market frenzy abated towards the end of 2009, but not for long. Between November 2014 and the summer of 2015, the Shanghai Composite doubled once again. Once again, animal spirits were stoked by Beijing, this time to offset weakness in the housing market. The central bank lowered its benchmark rate and expanded its own balance sheet. After restrictions on brokers’ loans were relaxed, margin loans grew to exceed $1 trillion.[38](#section-53) Technology shares sold for more than two hundred times earnings, ‘making the heady days of the dot-com bubble look tame by comparison’.[39](#section-53) The IPO of China National Nuclear Power in early June was oversubscribed by 137 times, locking up $273 billion in subscriptions. The shares increased by 44 per cent on the first day’s trading.

This speculative fever was also short-lived. By July 2015, the Shanghai Composite was down by a third. Trading halts were declared for a majority of stocks. Fearful of a complete market rout, Beijing strove to create an environment of ‘positive energy’. Regulators and censors warned citizens against making negative comments about the economy. The central bank cut interest rates and bank reserve requirements, and lent money to prop up the market. A ‘national team’ of state enterprises borrowed large sums to buy shares.[fn6](#section-58) At the graduation ceremony at Tsinghua University, students were instructed to ‘shout loudly the slogan, “revive the A shares, benefit the people; revive the A shares, benefit the people.”’[40](#section-53)

The ups and downs of the stock market were a sideshow compared to developments in China’s property market. During the global financial crisis, house prices dipped sharply in Beijing and other leading cities. The authorities acted forcefully to turn the tide. Banks were ordered to ease lending standards and provide more second mortgages. Housebuyers were able to borrow at a large discount to the benchmark rate. Over the course of 2009, mortgage lending quintupled and property sales rose by two-thirds.[41](#section-53) The *Wall Street Journal* reported on a rush to buy land in Beijing. House prices in Tier 1 cities – the world’s hottest real estate, according to Savills – climbed by more than two-thirds.

China overtook the United States to become the world’s largest property market by value.[42](#section-53) At which point, the authorities decided to cool the housing market. Interest rates and bank capital requirements were hiked in early 2010 and mortgage standards tightened. Banks were instructed to stop lending for third-home purchases.[43](#section-53) It took a while for these measures to bite, but towards the end of 2011 property prices were falling in nearly all of the seventy cities tracked by the National Bureau of Statistics. House sales crashed in Shanghai and Beijing. Whereupon policy was reversed again. In the summer of 2012, interest rates were cut as part of a ‘global coordinated global easing campaign’ (according to Bloomberg) linked to Europe’s sovereign debt crisis.

Having survived numerous setbacks, China’s property market gained a reputation for invincibility – a key condition, according to hedge fund tycoon George Soros, for a ‘super bubble’ to emerge. After the 2015 stock market crash, monetary policy was further eased. In October, the central bank’s benchmark rate reached an all-time low of 2 per cent. Over the following year, bank lending accelerated, with mortgages taking a greater share of new loans.[44](#section-53) In parts of Shanghai and neighbouring Suzhou, empty development plots sold for more than neighbouring land with completed buildings – a case of ‘flour more expensive than bread’. By late 2016, house prices were valued nationwide at eight times average Chinese incomes, roughly double the peak valuation of US housing a decade earlier.

Property valuations in China weren’t completely irrational. Sir James Steuart’s claim that the value of the Mississippi Company was justified by the low cost of borrowing applied to China’s real estate market. John Law’s Royal Bank set interest rates at 2 per cent in 1719. Nearly three centuries later, the People’s Bank set interest rates at the same level. A study released in 2015 by the National Bureau of Economic Research found that rental yields in Beijing and Shanghai had fallen below 2 per cent – in line with the discount rate.[45](#section-53) However, rental yields of less than 2 per cent implied a payback of nearly seven decades – roughly the same length of time as residential land leases, after which title reverted to the state. China’s property market was hailed as the ‘bubble that never pops’.[46](#section-53) But, as the NBER researchers commented, ‘only modest declines in expected appreciation seem needed to generate large drops in house values.’

By late 2016 total real estate was valued at $43 trillion, equivalent to nearly four times GDP and on a par with the aggregate value of Japanese real estate (relative to GDP) at its bubble peak.[47](#section-53) Like Japan three decades earlier, China had transformed into a ‘land bubble’ economy. The French bank Société Générale had calculated back in 2011 that over the previous decade China had built 16 billion square metres of residential floor space. This was equivalent to building modern Rome from scratch every fourteen days, over and over again. A decade after the stimulus more than half of the world’s hundred tallest buildings were under construction in the People’s Republic, and more than a quarter of economic output was related, directly or indirectly, to real estate development.[48](#section-53)

The ostensible rationale for China’s incredible building spree was urban migration. Yet while hordes of migrants worked on construction sites, they couldn’t afford to acquire the properties they built. Instead, much of the demand for new homes came from investors. In November 2009, Melissa Chan of Al Jazeera TV reported on the new development of Ordos (also known as Kangbashi) in Inner Mongolia.[49](#section-53) Built in five years, the city was intended to house over a million people. However, when Chan visited Ordos she found nothing but ‘empty homes, new and neat, block after block’. The apartments had reportedly been snapped up by rich Mongolian miners as investments. Overnight, Ordos became the world’s most famous ‘ghost city’.

Many new apartments in China were sold as concrete shells, known as ‘blank houses’ (*maopeifang*), that lacked basic amenities such as electric wiring and plumbing. Many remained in this unoccupied state for years on end. Absentee apartment owners saved money by not servicing elevators, which led to the occasional tragic accident.[fn7](#section-58) Vacant residential blocks could be identified at night by their darkened windows. In 2010, it was widely reported that some 65 million properties connected to the power grid were not using any electricity.[50](#section-53) Later estimates suggested that a fifth of the urban housing stock remained unoccupied.[51](#section-53) China was said to have enough empty properties to house the entire population of Canada.[52](#section-53)

China’s real estate bubble threatened the country’s economic miracle, by lowering productivity growth and fuelling corruption.[53](#section-53) As a retired senior Beijing official described the situation: ‘The real estate industry’s excessive prosperity has not only kidnapped local governments but also kidnapped financial institutions – restraining and even harming the development of the real economy, inflating asset bubbles and accumulating debt risk.’[54](#section-53) Real estate was the one thing in China more powerful than its imperial President. In December 2016, Xi Jinping proclaimed that ‘houses are for living in, not for speculation.’ Yet at the time nearly a third of Chinese families owned one or more vacant properties.[55](#section-53) Such was the nation’s devotion to property that the divorce rate spiked after Beijing imposed restrictions on families owning more than a single property.[56](#section-53)

### UNCOORDINATED INVESTMENT

Beijing’s stimulus plan launched thousands of ‘shovel-ready’ projects for new airports, bridges, highways, subways, and so forth. The most ambitious scheme involved the rapid expansion of the high-speed rail network, reportedly the world’s most expensive public works project since the US interstate highways were built in the 1950s.[57](#section-53) The person in charge of this mega-project was Railway Minister Liu Zhijun, whose Maoist exhortation that ‘To achieve a great leap, an entire generation must be sacrificed’ earned him the sobriquet ‘Great Leap Liu’. Spending on the project amounted to 2 per cent of China’s GDP.

By 2010, the Railway Ministry owed more than 1 trillion yuan on railway bonds alone. Alongside the inevitable cost overruns, there were rumours that cheap materials had been used by contractors, a practice known as ‘robbing the beams to put in the pillar’. Safety fears came to a head on 23 July 2011, when a bullet train bound for Fuzhou collided with another train outside Wenzhou, killing forty passengers and injuring many more. By this date, Liu was under investigation for ‘severe violations of discipline’. The Minister had received kickbacks on construction contracts, operated a slush fund to bribe newspaper editors and maintained no fewer than eighteen mistresses. (In July 2013 a court sentenced the former rail chief to death, commuted to life imprisonment.)

The legacy of the high-speed rail expansion was a massive waste of resources, mountains of debt, an economy addicted to construction spending, and public corruption on an epic scale. Writ large, this is the story of China’s recent economic development. When the cost of borrowing is low enough, even the most absurd investments can appear viable. In twenty-first-century China, easy money levelled mountains. Or, more precisely, the local government in the city of Shiyan, Hubei province, ordered that local mountains be flattened to make space for new manufacturing plants. ‘Levelling mountains,’ declared the local land bureau, ‘has become the golden key to resolve the problem of Shiyan’s development impasse.’[58](#section-53)

Spending on infrastructure normally tracks economic development: bridges are built, tunnels dug and railway tracks laid because there is an existing demand for their services. In China, however, investment plans were lifted from the *Field of Dreams*’ script: ‘if you build it, he will come.’ New infrastructure would supposedly drive urbanization and boost productivity. But researchers at Oxford’s business school found that ‘Far from being an engine of economic growth, a typical infrastructure investment has destroyed economic value in China.’[59](#section-53)

Among the other high-profile infrastructure projects at this time were a new airport south of Beijing said to be the size of Bermuda, and the world’s longest bridge, linking Hong Kong to the Mainland. China’s mandarins have a long tradition of authorizing impressive investments. The Grand Canal, the world’s longest waterway, was built in the seventh century with the forced labour of millions. ‘What is to be wondered at in China,’ wrote the Dominican monk Gaspar da Cruz in the sixteenth century, ‘is that there are bridges in uninhabited places throughout the country, and these are not less well built nor less costly than those which are nigh the cities, but rather they are all costly and very well wrought.’[60](#section-53) In the Immobile Empire some things never change.

Investment wasn’t merely directed towards infrastructure projects. As part of the stimulus, Beijing endorsed a ‘strategic emerging industries’ plan, promoting investment in new technologies, including biotech and electric vehicles.[61](#section-53) A number of sectors, ranging from aerospace to telecoms, were earmarked for ‘indigenous innovation’.[62](#section-53) Several ‘engineering mega-projects’ were fast-tracked, including a plan to develop a large-scale civilian jet-liner. Less glamorous industries were also supported with stimulus funds, including machinery, textiles, shipbuilding, car-making, steel, nonferrous metals and logistics. The trouble was that most of these industries already produced more than they could sell.[63](#section-53)

The glut in China’s steel production was notorious. Before the financial crisis, the People’s Republic produced around half of the world’s steel at a time when its steel companies were operating at just two-thirds of capacity.[64](#section-53) The boom in real estate and infrastructure created a much-needed surge in the demand for steel. But all the extra investment in steel plants meant supply continued to outstrip demand. Steel prices collapsed, falling to the point where it was said that ‘steel was cheaper than cabbage’.[fn8](#section-58)

A number of other industries, including cement, flat glass, paper, solar and wind power, were likewise afflicted by the twin scourges of overinvestment and oversupply.[65](#section-53) As with steel, the stimulus pushed cement demand through the roof. A much-cited factoid from the US Geological Survey claimed that in the three years after 2008 China consumed nearly one and a half times as much cement as the United States had used over the course of the twentieth century. On an annual basis, nearly two tonnes of cement were poured for every man, woman and child in the world’s most populous country.[66](#section-53) Nevertheless, China’s cement industry continued to be plagued with excess capacity and continued to add yet more capacity.

State-owned enterprises received the lion’s share of cheap bank credit, together with numerous other subsidies.[fn9](#section-58) But their access to low-cost capital had a negative impact on returns on capital. By 2014 state-owned enterprises were earning just half as much as their private counterparts.[67](#section-53) As their asset base expanded, their profitability declined.[68](#section-53)

As in Europe, China’s economy became infested with corporate zombies, nourished on a diet of cheap credit, state subsidies and loan forbearance.
