## Footnotes

### Introduction

[fn1](#section-11) Besides the ‘fructification theory’ (where interest is said to ‘derive’ from rent on land), there’s the surplus value (or profits) theory, productivity theory, ‘use theory’, ‘abstinence theory’ (spur to savings), ‘remuneration theories’, exploitation theory, reproductive theory and a number of Böhm-Bawerk’s ‘colourless theories’. To this list we should add Keynes’s notion, elaborated in his *General Theory*, that interest is required to discourage the hoarding of capital. Böhm-Bawerk rejected these explanations for interest, suggesting instead that interest arises because of man’s innate preference to enjoy present over future consumption. Needless to say, some economists deny the ‘time preference’ theory of interest.

[fn2](#section-11) Böhm-Bawerk was adamant on this point. Fisher, however, could conceive of situations when an individual’s time preference might turn negative. For instance, at times when incomes were declining rapidly, Fisher imagined that, if the stock of food was composed of spoiling figs, instead of hard tack, then the interest rate would be negative.

### 1: Babylonian Birth

[fn1](#section-13) Such folk, claims Mauss, were not motivated by ‘the cold reasoning of the merchant, the banker, and the capitalist … they repay with interest, but this is in order to humiliate the person initially making the gift or exchange, and not only to recompense him for loss caused to him by “deferred consumption”’ (Marcel Mauss, *The Gift: The Form and Reason for Exchange in Archaic Societies*, trans. W. D. Halls (London, 1990), pp. 96–7).

[fn2](#section-13) Marx calls Arnd’s theory the ‘primordial forest rate of interest’ (Marx, *Capital*, vol. III, trans. Samuel Moore and Edward Aveling (London, 1974), p. 363 fn).

[fn3](#section-13) Silver loans were made by weight, and barley loans by volume. One mina of barley was worth 60 shekels. Interest on silver was paid at the rate of one shekel per mina (1/60th per month or 20 per cent a year). There was a fixed exchange rate between barley and silver.

[fn4](#section-13) Assuming 20 per cent interest, paid annually and capitalized, Leemans calculates that the loan principal doubles with interest over 3 years and 283⅓ days (W. F. Leemans, *The Old Babylonian Merchant: His Business and His Social Position* (Leiden, 1950), p. 15).

[fn5](#section-13) There is no evidence that Einstein ever made this comment. The first known reference, according to the Quote Investigator website, is an advertisement for The Equity Savings & Loan Company published in the *Cleveland Plain Dealer* of Ohio in 1925: ‘The Eighth Wonder of the World – is compound interest. It does things to money. At the Equity it doubles your money every 14 years’ (<https://quoteinvestigator.com/2019/09/09/interest/>).

[fn6](#section-13) William Goetzmann comments that this is equivalent to 580 times the annual barley harvest of the United States (William Goetzmann, *Money Changes Everything: How Finance Made Civilization Possible* (Princeton, 2016), p. 35).

[fn7](#section-13) Clean slates limited the social disturbances that arose when borrowers fell into a state of debt bondage or had their lands foreclosed by creditors. *Misarum* acts only touched upon consumer (grain) loans, while commercial (silver) debts were unaffected. This suggests that the rulers were mostly concerned with the social consequences of excessive personal debt (Michael Hudson, ‘Reconstructing the origins of interest-bearing debt and the logic of clean slates’, in *Debt and Economic Renewal in the Ancient Near East*, eds. Michael Hudson and Marc van der Mieroop (Bethesda, Md, 2002), p. 7).

[fn8](#section-13) Morris Silver, *Economic Structures of Antiquity* (Westport, Conn., 1995), ch. 5 *passim*. Although it has been claimed that Ancient Greece lacked a true money market, a decree issued in the late fifth century BC by Plotheia, a district of Attica, calls for money to be lent out to borrowers offering the highest interest rate.

[fn9](#section-13) It is curious to note that the chief beneficiaries of Tiberius’ quantitative easing were patrician families. As we shall see, this was also the case when the Federal Reserve revived the practice in 2008.

### 2: Selling Time

[fn1](#section-14) ‘Debt was a deliberate device,’ writes Sir Moses Finley, ‘on the part of the creditor to obtain more dependent labour rather than a device for enrichment through interest’ (Finley, *Economy and Society in Ancient Greece* (London, 1981), p. 156).

[fn2](#section-14) Interest-free loans were available in Ancient Athens. Known as *eranos* loans, they were supplied by groups of lenders to be repaid when funds became available. Demosthenes claimed that the slave-prostitute Neara bought her freedom by raising *eranos* contributions from former clients.

[fn3](#section-14) Bonaventura’s comment contains the germ of Marx’s ‘labour theory of value’. In contradiction, Böhm-Bawerk pointed out that a bottle of wine, placed in the cellar, increases in value without any additional labour input.

[fn4](#section-14) Double-entry bookkeeping represents an extraordinary intellectual feat of quantification. Every asset and each exchange is given a monetary value and recorded in the same currency. The use of Arabic numerals enabled figures to be readily calculated. The German sociologist Werner Sombart, author of the six volume *Modern Capitalism* (first published in 1912), went so far as to claim that, by encouraging regular record-keeping, mathematical order and the reduction of events to numerical abstractions, double-entry contains the germ of the later Scientific Revolution.

[fn5](#section-14) Adam Smith, *An Inquiry into The Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations* [1776] (London, 1875), p. 44. Also, p. 285: ‘It may be laid down as a maxim, that wherever a great deal can be made by the use of money, a great deal will commonly be given for the use of it … Accordingly, therefore, as the usual market rate of interest varies in any country, we may be assured that the ordinary profits of stock must vary with it, must sink as it sinks, and rise as it rises.’

[fn6](#section-14) See Henri Eugene Sée, *Modern Capitalism* (New York, 1928), p. 125. Sée writes: ‘The present day meaning of *capital* was expressed, in the seventeenth century, by the word *principal*, or by the word *interest*. For example, such an expression as the following was used: “to take an interest of 5000 *livres* in a business.” Only in the course of the eighteenth century did the word capital really begin to take on its present meaning.’

[fn7](#section-14) Lionel Robbins, *A History of Economic Thought* (Princeton, 1998), p. 54. Ludwig von Mises made a similar point, writing in ‘Human Action: The Rate of Interest’ that anyone ‘who wants to “abolish” interest will have to induce people to value an apple available in a hundred years no less than a present apple’.

### 3: The Lowering of Interest

[fn1](#section-15) In *The Nature and Necessity of Interest* (London, 1903), Gustav Cassel calls Child’s comment an ‘evident absurdity’.

[fn2](#section-15) ‘As their critics pointed out, the directors [of the East India Company] maximized their return by refusing to issue more stock and trading on short-term, borrowed capital … they could profit, without investing more of their own capital, from the difference between the interest which they paid on bonds and the net profits of the trade. In 1683, however, a shortage of working capital created a temporary financial crisis. The stock fell in value and the company was forced to raise the rate on its bonds to 5 per cent in order to attract capital’ (extract from Sir Josiah Child’s entry in the *Oxford Dictionary of National Biography*).

[fn3](#section-15) Locke writes that ‘If lessening use [interest] to four per cent. should at all alter the quantity of money, and make it less, it would make money, as it has the nature of a commodity, dearer’ (*Some Considerations of the Consequences of the Lowering of Interest and the Raising of the Value of Money* [London, 1691], in *On Money*, vol. I (Oxford, 1991), p. 257).

[fn4](#section-15) Some of Child’s wilder ideas are still with us. ‘Low interest rates can cause a baby boom, Bank of England suggests’ ran the headline of an article in the *Daily Telegraph* on 23 December 2019.

### 4: The Chimera

[fn1](#section-16) The Genoese bank was created in 1407 by consolidating funded loans and distributing shares, *luoghi*, whose dividends varied with the tax yield. Law maintained an account with the Casa di San Giorgio, which he considered the ‘best governed [bank] in Italy’ (James Buchan, *John Law* (London, 2018), p. 81).

[fn2](#section-16) In Hamilton’s view, France’s ‘huge funded debt, the depreciated paper currency, and the acute commercial crisis were largely responsible for France’s acceptance of John Law’s scheme’. (See Earl J. Hamilton, ‘Prices and Wages at Paris under John Law’s System’, *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 51(1), 1936, and ‘The Origin and Growth of the National Debt in Western Europe’, *American Economic Review*, 122, 1947.)

[fn3](#section-16) The issue at 500 livres in late 1718 was followed by another at 550 in the following June, rising to 1,000 in the next month, and 5,000 livres for the issues of September and October of 1719.

[fn4](#section-16) In the second half of 1719 only a 10 per cent down-payment was required on new issues. Subscribers were in effect buying options.

[fn5](#section-16) At this time a mason earned around 170 livres a year. The median US income is currently close to $59,000. Based on these relative incomes, Law paid close to $350 million in today’s currency for the Palais Mazarin. The building became the headquarters of the Company and the Royal Bank, and later housed France’s Bibliothèque Nationale.

[fn6](#section-16) When Law first approached the Regent with his scheme, the banker Samuel Bernard advised against it, saying there was ‘no foundation for the bank he proposes, in a country where everything depends on the King’s pleasure’ (Buchan, *John Law*, p. 111).

[fn7](#section-16) The definition of ‘realize’ is Washington Irving’s (from his 1825 essay, ‘The Great Mississippi Bubble’). An edict of December 1719 decreed that all public payments must be made in bank notes. The following February the import and wearing of precious metals, diamonds and pearls was banned and the Company was given the powers to search for hoarded coins. By the end of the month, only regulated goldsmiths were allowed to possess gold and silver.

[fn8](#section-16) Buchan writes that Law is invoking a ‘new species of property, where your capital is of use to the entire body of the nation’. Law’s autocratic desire to prevent money-hoarding foreshadows recent calls to abolish physical cash, to stop money being hoarded, at a time when central banks were attempting to impose negative interest rates (Buchan, *John Law*, p. 271).

[fn9](#section-16) ‘Law’s easy credit policy must have been largely responsible,’ wrote Hamilton, ‘for the failure of the market rate of interest to rise during the Bubble. In conformity with Wicksell’s theory, the disparity between the natural and the market rates of interest accentuated credit expansion and played an important role in the sharp upswing of prices’ (‘Prices and Wages at Paris under John Law’s System’, p. 63; see also François Velde, ‘John Law’s System’, *American Economic Review*, 97 (2), 2007).

[fn10](#section-16) In his ‘Essay on the Land Bank’ (written around 1704), Law criticized the rival land bank scheme of Hugh Chamberlen, who proposed supplying £10,000 of bank notes against land collateral, yielding an annual income of just £150 (i.e. a capitalization rate of 1.5 per cent), and attacked John Briscoe’s plan for a land bank which mooted an even lower lending rate.

[fn11](#section-16) That inflationary forces initially raise prices in some parts of the economy before becoming more widespread is known as the ‘Cantillon effect’.

### 7: Goodhart’s Law

[fn1](#section-20) Although this book argues that price stability shouldn’t be the sole aim of monetary policy, this is not to say that inflation is desirable. The case against inflation is so well known it hardly needs recalling. Inflation damages economic growth by interfering with price signals and hindering long-term planning. It also distorts profits in myriad ways. Unanticipated inflation involves an unfair redistribution of income and wealth.

At an earlier meeting in the White House, President Johnson told Martin that raising rates would ‘amount to squeezing blood from the American working man in the interest of Wall Street’. In the end, Martin kept the punch bowl in place for too long and inflation took off under his watch (Paul Volcker and Christine Harper, *Keeping at It: The Quest for Sound Money and Good Government* (New York, 2018), p. 55).

[fn3](#section-20) Greta Kippner, *Capitalizing on Crisis: The Political Origins of the Rise of Finance* (London, 2011), p. 113. Henceforth, the Fed found that raising interest rates was politically more difficult.

And to do that, as Paul McCulley of PIMCO put it, Alan Greenspan needs to create a housing bubble to replace the Nasdaq bubble …’ Krugman apparently found nothing wrong with this suggestion (Paul Krugman, ‘Dubya’s Double Dip?’, *New York Times*, 2 August 2002).

Bernanke’s argument was based on a recently published paper by Fed researchers (Jane Dokko *et al.,* ‘Monetary Policy and the Housing Bubble’, Federal Reserve Board, 22 December 2009). The paper’s authors claim that low rates in 2003–4 were justified on a precautionary basis due to the ‘significant risk’ of deflation (although they admit that subsequent revisions to inflation statistics showed deflation risk was exaggerated). Besides, they say, the Fed was only acting in a conventional fashion: the ‘setting of monetary policy appeared to follow the broad contours that would be expected given conventional macroeconomic views … outside forecasters, on balance, saw the policy stance adopted by the FOMC as consistent with the FOMC’s objectives’ ([p. 13](#section-13)). They claim, rather disingenuously, that the US housing ‘boom’ started in 1998, long before the easy money policy commenced (as we’ve noted above, US house prices only exceeded 2 standard deviations above trend after 2002). The authors conclude that ‘all told, the evidence appears mixed at best on whether the policy stance of advanced economy central banks is among the significant factors contributing to the run-up in housing.’

That at the same time such issues have the effect of destroying the steering mechanism of the market is not so easily seen. But supplies of such funds for additional purchases of goods produce a distortion of the structure of relative prices which draws resources into activities that cannot be lastingly maintained and thereby become the cause of an inevitable later reaction.’

As William White comments (in a personal email to the author): central bankers make a profound epistemological error by failing to treat the economy as a complex adaptive system. All their other errors are derivative.

If interest rates are destined to be at low levels … [i]t makes any stream of earnings from investments worth more money. The bogey is always what government bonds yield.’

[fn2](#section-34) Keynes had argued that people hoarded money because they expected a higher rate of interest in future. ‘Thus,’ wrote Robertson, ‘the rate of interest is what it is because it is expected to become other than it is; if it is not expected to become other than it is, there is nothing left to tell why it is – the organ which secretes it has been amputated, and yet somehow still exists – a grin without a cat.’

### Introduction

[fn1](#section-11) Besides the ‘fructification theory’ (where interest is said to ‘derive’ from rent on land), there’s the surplus value (or profits) theory, productivity theory, ‘use theory’, ‘abstinence theory’ (spur to savings), ‘remuneration theories’, exploitation theory, reproductive theory and a number of Böhm-Bawerk’s ‘colourless theories’. To this list we should add Keynes’s notion, elaborated in his *General Theory*, that interest is required to discourage the hoarding of capital. Böhm-Bawerk rejected these explanations for interest, suggesting instead that interest arises because of man’s innate preference to enjoy present over future consumption. Needless to say, some economists deny the ‘time preference’ theory of interest.

[fn2](#section-11) Böhm-Bawerk was adamant on this point. Fisher, however, could conceive of situations when an individual’s time preference might turn negative. For instance, at times when incomes were declining rapidly, Fisher imagined that, if the stock of food was composed of spoiling figs, instead of hard tack, then the interest rate would be negative.

### 6: Un Petit Coup de Whisky

[fn1](#section-18) Treasury Secretary Shaw, who served under Teddy Roosevelt between 1902 and 1907, was said to conceive of only three evils: ‘high interest rates, a decline in the prices of stocks, and a contraction of credit, but these evils, in his opinion, were so serious that they were to be corrected at whatever cost.’ The author of this comment blamed successive Treasury secretaries for resisting with ‘all the vast resources of the government treasury the natural tendency of interest rates to follow the rising level of prices. The answer is that intervening credit boom and various asset price bubbles had rendered its financial system unstable. ### 7: Goodhart’s Law

[fn1](#section-20) Although this book argues that price stability shouldn’t be the sole aim of monetary policy, this is not to say that inflation is desirable. The case against inflation is so well known it hardly needs recalling. Inflation damages economic growth by interfering with price signals and hindering long-term planning. It also distorts profits in myriad ways. Unanticipated inflation involves an unfair redistribution of income and wealth.

[fn2](#section-20) During his time at the Fed, Martin was bullied by President Lyndon B. Johnson to keep interest rates low. In December 1965, the Fed Chairman visited Johnson at his Texas ranch. The President took Martin for a fast drive in his jeep over a rough track in order to soften Martin up and induce him to cut interest rates. At an earlier meeting in the White House, President Johnson told Martin that raising rates would ‘amount to squeezing blood from the American working man in the interest of Wall Street’. In the end, Martin kept the punch bowl in place for too long and inflation took off under his watch (Paul Volcker and Christine Harper, *Keeping at It: The Quest for Sound Money and Good Government* (New York, 2018), p. 55).

[fn3](#section-20) Greta Kippner, *Capitalizing on Crisis: The Political Origins of the Rise of Finance* (London, 2011), p. 113. Kippner suggests that the Fed changed its policy after the October crash in order to use interest rates to support financial markets and to provide greater transparency and predictability. Henceforth, the Fed found that raising interest rates was politically more difficult.

[fn4](#section-20) The idea of creating a bubble to deal with a bubble had earlier been mooted by Paul Krugman in the *New York Times* in August 2002: ‘To fight this recession the Fed needs more than a snapback; it needs soaring household spending to offset moribund business investment. And to do that, as Paul McCulley of PIMCO put it, Alan Greenspan needs to create a housing bubble to replace the Nasdaq bubble …’ Krugman apparently found nothing wrong with this suggestion (Paul Krugman, ‘Dubya’s Double Dip?’, *New York Times*, 2 August 2002).

[fn5](#section-20) Ben Bernanke, ‘Monetary Policy and the Housing Bubble’, speech at the Annual Meeting of the American Economic Association, 3 January 2010. ‘Monetary policy following the 2001 recession appears to have been reasonably appropriate, at least in relation to a simple policy rule.’ This begs the question of whether the ‘simple policy rule’ was appropriate.

[fn6](#section-20) Bernanke, ‘Monetary Policy and the Housing Bubble’. Bernanke’s argument was based on a recently published paper by Fed researchers (Jane Dokko *et al.,* ‘Monetary Policy and the Housing Bubble’, Federal Reserve Board, 22 December 2009). The paper’s authors claim that low rates in 2003–4 were justified on a precautionary basis due to the ‘significant risk’ of deflation (although they admit that subsequent revisions to inflation statistics showed deflation risk was exaggerated). Besides, they say, the Fed was only acting in a conventional fashion: the ‘setting of monetary policy appeared to follow the broad contours that would be expected given conventional macroeconomic views … outside forecasters, on balance, saw the policy stance adopted by the FOMC as consistent with the FOMC’s objectives’ ([p. 13](#section-13)). They claim, rather disingenuously, that the US housing ‘boom’ started in 1998, long before the easy money policy commenced (as we’ve noted above, US house prices only exceeded 2 standard deviations above trend after 2002). The authors conclude that ‘all told, the evidence appears mixed at best on whether the policy stance of advanced economy central banks is among the significant factors contributing to the run-up in housing.’

This is discussed in more detail in [Chapter 17](#section-31).

Summers added that ‘low nominal and real interest rates undermine financial stability in various ways. They increase risk-taking as investors reach for yield, promote irresponsible lending as coupon obligations become very low and easy to meet, and make Ponzi financial structures more attractive as interest rates look low relative to expected growth rates.’ (See L. Summers, ‘Reflections on the New Secular Stagnation Hypothesis’, in *Secular Stagnation, Facts, Causes and Cures*, eds. C. Teulings and R. Baldwin (London, 2014), pp. 32–3.)

[fn8](#section-28) According to Stein, ‘low interest rates increase the demand by agents to engage in below-the-radar forms of risk-taking, this demand may prompt innovations that facilitate this sort of risk-taking’ (Jeremy Stein, ‘Overheating in Credit Markets: Origins, Measurement, and Policy Responses’, speech at the Federal Reserve Board, 7 February 2013).

[fn9](#section-28) In *The City of London*, vol. III (p. 391), David Kynaston describes a meeting of the Committee of London Clearing Bankers in November 1936, held at the Bank of England, where Governor Montagu Norman raised his eyebrows: ‘The Governor referred to the recent rise in Stock Exchange prices and the possibility of the existence of a position of over-speculation. While there was, in his opinion, no need at the moment for action he asked the bankers to watch the position carefully and to report to him in a month or two.’

[fn10](#section-28) In 2013, JP Morgan Chase announced it would hire some 13,000 extra compliance staff, at a cost of $4 billion. By the end of 2014, Citigroup was expected to employ more than 30,000 compliance officers (Sital Patel, ‘Citi Will Have Almost 30,000 Employees in Compliance by Year-End’, *MarketWatch*, 14 July 2014).

[fn11](#section-28) As Hyman Minsky observed, most financial innovation is intended to get around the regulations put in place after the last crisis. In this way, financial regulation resembles the Maginot Line, built by the French after the Great War to protect against another German invasion. During the Second World War, the German army simply bypassed this massive fortification by going through the supposedly impenetrable forests of the Ardennes.

### 16: Rusting Money

[fn1](#section-29) Banks use ‘risk-free’ US Treasuries as collateral for financial transactions known as repos. As the Fed’s QE reduced the float of Treasuries, these bonds weren’t available to be lent out or rehypothecated to foster private credit growth (see Gross, ‘Wounded Heart’, PIMCO Insights, 4 June 2013).

[fn2](#section-29) The fact that interest is necessary to get people to lend was observed by the early economists. As the merchant-economist Sir Dudley North wrote in the 1690s, ‘high Interest will bring Money out from Hoards, Plate, &c., into Trade, when low Interest will keep it back.’

[fn3](#section-29) On the deflationary impact of zombies see Viral V. Acharya *et al*., ‘Zombie Credit and (Dis-)Inflation: Evidence from Europe’, NBER Working Paper, May 2020. This paper claims that providing loss-making firms with credit resulted in excess capacity, which, in turn, ‘puts downward pressure on markups and product prices and thereby lowers inflation’.

[fn4](#section-29) Changes in household debt varied by nation. Between 2000 and 2008, US household debt climbed by 25 percentage points relative to GDP, and fell by 20 percentage points over the following decade. UK household debt followed a similar trajectory. In both countries, household deleveraging created a deflationary headwind. In several other advanced economies (including Sweden, Canada and Australia) consumer debt rose to record levels after 2008 (data from the BIS).

### 17: The Mother and Father of All Evil

[fn1](#section-31) Cross-border lending financed an overseas acquisition spree by Icelandic bankers, which included a faded English football club, a famous London toy store and a second-tier UK supermarket (coincidentally named Iceland). After accounting for the value of its foreign assets, Iceland’s net foreign debts amounted to twice its national income. The influx of foreign capital funded a current account deficit equivalent to a quarter of Icelandic GDP.

[fn2](#section-31) On 7 August 2007, the French bank BNP Paribas suspended redemptions on three funds that owned US mortgage securities. Cut off from the international capital markets, Northern Rock, a mid-sized British bank, closed its doors a few months later. Northern Rock’s was the first English bank run since Overend Gurney’s collapse of 1866. (See Viral Acharya and Sascha Steffen, ‘The Banking Crisis as a Giant Carry Trade Gone Wrong’, *VoxEu*, 23 May 2013.)

[fn3](#section-31) Jeremy Grantham, ‘Time to Wake Up: Days of Abundant Resources and Falling Prices are Over Forever’, GMO Quarterly Letter, April 2011. At the time of publication, the following industrial commodities were more than two standard deviations above their long-term price trend: lead (2.4 s.d.), platinum (2.4), oil (2.5), gold (2.6), nickel (2.7), palladium (3.4), silver (3.7), copper (3.9), coal (4.1) and iron ore (4.9).

[fn4](#section-31) The radical economist Henry George saw a connection between interest rates and wages, which arose from the competition between capital and labour: ‘interest,’ wrote George, ‘cannot be increased without increasing wages; nor wages lowered without depressing interest. For if wages fall, interest must also fall in proportion, else it becomes more profitable to turn labor into capital than to apply it directly; while, if interest falls, wages must likewise proportionately fall, or else the increment of capital would be checked.’ This is a keen insight. (Henry George, *Progress and Poverty* (New York, 1923), p. 199.)

[fn5](#section-31) In the five years after China joined the Word Trade Organization in 2001, manufacturing employment in Britain and the United States declined by a third. Displaced workers appear to have found less-well-paid, lower productivity jobs elsewhere. See Stewart Paterson, *China, Trade and Power: Why the West’s Economic Engagement Has Failed* (London, 2018).

[fn6](#section-31) By 2018, the US had a negative net international investment position of $10 trillion, a fivefold increase since before the financial crisis.

### 18: Financial Repression with Chinese Characteristics

[fn1](#section-32) Lien-sheng Yang, *Money and Credit in China: A Short History* (Cambridge, Mass., 1952), p. 97. The traditional reluctance of the Chinese state to pay interest is summed up in the comment of a late Qing official who stated that ‘as the loan is one from people to officials, it is inexpedient that it should bear interest.’

[fn2](#section-32) Richard von Glahn, *Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000–1700* (London, 1996), p. 1. Glahn writes that ‘The state exercised greater direct control over money than over virtually any other facet of the economy, particularly since Chinese political economy deemed monetary policy the single most important tool of economic management at the ruler’s disposal.’

[fn3](#section-32) Between 1997 and 2002, bank deposits paid on average 3 per cent above the level of inflation. Over the following decade, the 1-year bank deposit rate, in real terms, averaged -0.3 per cent.

[fn4](#section-32) A 2010 BIS report states that ‘The household income share has also been dragged down by its shrinking net interest income. As a share of GDP, the net interest income halved in the past 15 years [to 2010], accounting for a quarter of the decline in the household income share’ (Guonan Ma and Wang Yi, ‘China’s High Saving Rate: Myth and Reality’, BIS Working Paper, June 2010, p. 18).

[fn5](#section-32) During this period there was a strong relationship between foreign capital inflows and the growth of deposits in the Chinese banking system.

[fn6](#section-32) By early September, the ‘national team’ of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) had spent an estimated 1.5 trillion yuan supporting the stock market, taking ownership of 9 per cent of the tradable shares (free float) on the mainland, according to Goldman Sachs. Other measures to support the market included a ban on short sales, forcing companies to engage in buybacks, strong-arming brokers into buying stocks, the relaxation of collateral rules on margin loans, and a halt to further IPOs. (See Kana Nishizawa, ‘China’s Stock-Rescue Tab Surges to $236 Billion, Goldman Says’, Bloomberg, 7 September 2015.)

[fn7](#section-32) The high occurrence of elevator accidents was partly due to the fact there were no condo associations in China and residents on lower floors often didn’t contribute towards elevator costs.

[fn8](#section-32) China’s steel consumption compounded at an annual rate of 15 per cent from 2000 to 2008 and maintained this growth level after the financial crisis. In 2009, steel consumption climbed by an astonishing 157 million tons. In 2017, the steel industry was operating at 70 per cent of capacity. (Dinny McMahon, *China’s Great Wall of Debt* (New York, 2018), p. 42; Nicholas Lardy, *Sustaining China’s Economic Growth after the Global Financial Crisis* (Washington, DC, 2012), p. 21; Thomas Orlik, *China: The Bubble That Never Pops* (New York, 2020), p. 14.)

Balding estimates that a 5 per cent interest charge would have reduced reported profits by nearly 40 per cent (Giovanni Ferri and Li-Gang Liu, ‘Honor thy Creditors before thy Shareholders: Are the Profits of Chinese State-owned Enterprises Real?’, *Asian Economic Papers*, 9 (3), October 2010; Christopher Balding, ‘Guest post: Sizing up NPL risk in China’, *Financial Times*, 28 October 2015; for other SOE subsidies, see Usha Haley and George Haley, *Subsidies to Chinese Industry* (Oxford, 2013), p. 45).

[fn11](#section-32) Reuters reported that Chinese companies owed a total of $18 trillion, equivalent to 169 per cent of the country’s GDP. Only a quarter of mainland companies listed in Hong Kong had sufficient profits to cover interest costs. Being an SOE also helps’ (Umesh Desai, ‘Road to Stagnation? China Inc Gets a Break from Lenders’, Reuters, 4 October 2016).

[fn14](#section-32) See Michael Pettis, ‘Why the Bezzle Matters to the Economy’, China Financial Markets, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 23 August 2021. Pettis argues that China’s bezzle includes the real estate market, where market values exceeding fundamental values created what Galbraith called a ‘net increase in psychic wealth’, and wasteful infrastructure projects that are entered at cost in the national income accounts. The total size of China’s bezzle, Pettis suggests, is roughly indicated by the country’s rising stock of unpayable debt.

### Conclusion

[fn1](#section-33) Even though US public debt climbed by over 40 per cent of GDP (2007–18), the government’s debt-service ratio was held at just over 2 per cent of GDP. In Japan, public debt doubled between 2000 and 2018, to reach nearly 250 per cent of GDP, but Japan’s debt-service ratio remained below 2 per cent of GDP. (See Charles Goodhart and Manoj Pradhan, *The Great Demographic Reversal* (Cham, Switzerland, 2020), p. 173.)

[fn2](#section-33) The Productive Finance Working Group was convened in November 2020 by the Bank of England, HM Treasury and the Financial Conduct Authority ‘to develop practical solutions to the barriers to investing in long-term, less liquid assets’.

[fn3](#section-33) Strangely enough, this is what the Canadian economist Robert Mundell, the ‘father of the Euro’, originally envisaged. Mundell claimed that the European single currency ‘puts monetary policy out of the reach of politicians’, with the effect that ‘[b]othersome democracy is removed from the economic system’ (Michael Hudson, *Killing the Host: How Financial Parasites and Debt Bondage Destroy the Global Economy* (Petrolia, Ontario, 2015), p. 326).

[fn4](#section-33) For instance, in *The Denationalisation of Money* (London, 1990), p. 104, Hayek writes that ‘loanable funds made artificially cheap by creating more money for lending them, not only help those to whom they are lent, though at the expense of others, but for a while have a general stimulating effect on business activity. That at the same time such issues have the effect of destroying the steering mechanism of the market is not so easily seen. But supplies of such funds for additional purchases of goods produce a distortion of the structure of relative prices which draws resources into activities that cannot be lastingly maintained and thereby become the cause of an inevitable later reaction.’

[fn5](#section-33) Keynes’s widow, Lydia, was one of the many rentiers whose fortune was swept away by the rising tide of post-war inflation.

[fn6](#section-33) F. A. Hayek, ‘The Pretence of Knowledge’, lecture given at the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel award ceremony, 11 December 1974. As William White comments (in a personal email to the author): central bankers make a profound epistemological error by failing to treat the economy as a complex adaptive system. All their other errors are derivative.

### Postscript

[fn1](#section-34) ‘Warren Buffett Wants to Make You Happier, Smarter and Richer’, Bloomberg, 2 May 2021. Three years earlier, Buffett had commented that ‘the most important item over time in valuation is obviously interest rates. If interest rates are destined to be at low levels … [i]t makes any stream of earnings from investments worth more money. The bogey is always what government bonds yield.’

[fn2](#section-34) Keynes had argued that people hoarded money because they expected a higher rate of interest in future. ‘Thus,’ wrote Robertson, ‘the rate of interest is what it is because it is expected to become other than it is; if it is not expected to become other than it is, there is nothing left to tell why it is – the organ which secretes it has been amputated, and yet somehow still exists – a grin without a cat.’
